title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
會試錄序
聖天子龍飛紀元之初適天下賓
興賢能之歲由是兩京暨十
三布政司之士領鄉書而會
試於春官者實倍於前太子
太傅掌部事臣瀠尚書臣寧
以考試官請
===
上命臣淵臣文往涖焉其同考則
臣儼臣紹臣琦臣傅臣槩臣
瑤臣翊臣崑監試則御史臣
清臣諫及諸執事皆祗奉惟
謹凡三試拔其文之中式者
若干人視舊額蓋又過之於
戲盛矣哉臣嘗觀夫天之生

會試録序
聖天子龍飛紀元之初適天下賔
興賢能之歲由是兩京暨十
三布政司之士領鄉書而會
試於春官者實倍於前太子
太傅掌部事臣濙尚書臣寧
以考試官請
===
上命臣淵臣文往涖焉其同考則
臣儼臣紹臣琦臣博臣崇本臣
珽臣翊臣崑監試則御史臣
清臣諫及諸執事皆祗奉惟
謹凡三試拔其文之中式者
若干人視舊額蓋又過之於
戲盛矣哉臣嘗觀夫天之生
punctuated:
會試錄序

聖天子龍飛紀元之初，適天下賓興賢能之歲。由是，兩京暨十三布政司之士，領鄉書而會試於春官者，實倍於前。太子太傅、掌部事臣瀠，尚書臣寧，以考試官請。上命臣淵、臣文往涖焉。其同考則臣儼、臣紹、臣琦、臣傅、臣槩、臣瑤、臣翊、臣崑；監試則御史臣清、臣諫，及諸執事，皆祗奉惟謹。凡三試，拔其文之中式者若干人，視舊額蓋又過之。於戲，盛矣哉！臣嘗觀夫天之生
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

At the beginning of the new reign era when the Sacred Son of Heaven ascended the dragon throne, it happened to be the year when the realm ceremonially recommends the worthy and capable. Consequently, the scholars from the two capitals and the thirteen Provincial Administration Commissions who received their letters of provincial recommendation and gathered for the Metropolitan Examination at the Ministry of Rites were indeed double the number of previous years. The Grand Mentor of the Heir Apparent managing the affairs of the Ministry, Your Servant Ying (Hu Ying 胡濙), and the Minister, Your Servant Ning (Yang Ning 楊寧), petitioned for the appointment of the Examiners. His Majesty commanded Your Servant Yuan (Jiang Yuan 江淵) and Your Servant Wen (Lin Wen 林文) to go and preside over it. As for the Associate Examiners—Your Servant Yan (Liu Yan 劉儼), Your Servant Shao (Lü Shao 呂紹), Your Servant Qi (Huang Qi 黃琦), Your Servant Fu (Wang Fu 王傅), Your Servant Gai (Wang Gai 王槩), Your Servant Yao (Zhang Yao 張瑤), Your Servant Yi (Yang Yi 楊翊), and Your Servant Kun (Chen Kun 陳崑)—the Monitoring Examiners, Censors Your Servant Qing (Zhou Qing 周清) and Your Servant Jian (Song Jian 宋諫), as well as all the officiating functionaries, all reverently and谨cently carried out their duties with utmost care. Across the three sessions of the examination, a certain number of candidates whose essays met the standard were selected, surpassing even the former quota. Oh, how magnificent! I have observed how Heaven gives birth to [the worthy]…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
賢有資於世用大矣彼南金
美玉天下之至寶也然非所
以益天下麒麟鳳凰天下之
禎祥也然非所以致太平而
所以益天下致太平者則惟
賢才焉經曰所寶惟賢此之
謂也惟昔聖帝明王知其然
===
故宵旰孜孜以得賢為務我
國家取人非一途亦惟以進士
科為尤重自洪武以来厯二
十餘科得士之多其間蜚聲
光邁偉烈者彬彬而盛内而
列孤卿登臺閣以之潤色
皇猷鋪張鴻業外而作牧守居方
alt_text:
賢有資於世用大矣彼南金
美玉天下之至寶也然非所
以益天下麒麟鳳凰天下之
禎祥也然非所以致太平而
所以益天下致太平者則惟
賢才焉經曰所寶惟賢此之
謂也惟昔聖帝明王知其然
===
故宵旰孜孜以得賢爲務我
國家取人非一途亦惟以進士
科爲尤重自洪武以來歷二
十餘科得士之多其間蜚聲
光邁偉烈者彬彬而盛內而
列孫卿登臺閣以之潤色
皇猷鋪張鴻業外而作牧守居方
punctuated: 賢，有資於世用大矣。彼南金、美玉，天下之至寶也，然非所以益天下；麒麟、鳳凰，天下之禎祥也，然非所以致太平。而所以益天下、致太平者，則惟賢才焉。《經》曰：「所寶惟賢。」此之謂也。惟昔聖帝明王知其然，故宵旰孜孜，以得賢為務。我國家取人非一途，亦惟以進士科為尤重。自洪武以来，厯二十餘科，得士之多，其間蜚聲光、邁偉烈者，彬彬而盛。内而列孤卿、登臺閣，以之潤色皇猷、鋪張鴻業；外而作牧守、居方
translation_en:
… the worthy, their contribution to the practical use of the world is great indeed! Now, southern gold and fine jade are the supreme treasures of the realm, yet they are not the means by which to benefit the realm; the unicorn and the phoenix are the auspicious omens of the realm, yet they are not the means by which to bring about great peace. Rather, that by which the realm is benefited and great peace is brought about is solely worthy talent. When the Classic says, "What is treasured is only the worthy," this is what it means. In antiquity, the sage emperors and enlightened kings knew this to be so; therefore, dressing before dawn and eating after dusk in tireless diligence, they made obtaining the worthy their priority.

Our Dynasty selects men through more than one avenue, yet it too places particular weight upon the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination. Since the Hongwu era (1368–1398), through more than twenty examinations, in the multitude of scholars obtained, those among them who have achieved illustrious renown and surpassed others in great deeds have been refined and abundant. At court, they take their places among the Three Solitaries and Nine Ministers or ascend to the Censorate and Grand Secretariat, thereby lending grace to the Imperial plans and unfolding the grand enterprise; in the provinces, they serve as prefects and department magistrates or occupy the posts of provincial…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
岳以之旬宣藩翰撫綏黎元
咸有其人則我
朝科目之得人視前代為有加
矣洪惟
皇上以大有為之資隆中興之業
而成太平之治既開解額又
親舉視學之典無非所以崇
===
儒重道作興賢才而為
國家之用也士際斯時階茲榮
幸可不奮庸以圖報稱茲又
登天府之籍進
大廷之對服官政躋顯融有日
矣尚其懋焉使儒者之效不
徒托諸空言而必見於天下

咸有其人則我
朝科目之得人視前代爲有加
矣洪惟
皇上以大有爲之資隆中興之業
而成太平之治既開解額又
親舉視學之典無非所以崇
===
儒重道作興賢才而爲
國家之用也士際斯時階茲榮
幸可不奮庸以圖報稱茲又
登天府之籍進
大廷之對服官政躋顯融有日
矣尚其懋焉使儒者之效不
徒托諸空言而必見於天下
punctuated: 岳，以之旬宣藩翰、撫綏黎元，咸有其人。則我朝科目之得人，視前代為有加矣。洪惟皇上以大有為之資，隆中興之業，而成太平之治。既開解額，又親舉視學之典，無非所以崇儒重道、作興賢才，而為國家之用也。士際斯時，階茲榮幸，可不奮庸以圖報稱？茲又登天府之籍，進大廷之對，服官政、躋顯融有日矣。尚其懋焉，使儒者之效不徒托諸空言，而必見於天下
translation_en:
… and the regional administration, using them to promulgate imperial virtue at the frontiers and bring peace and comfort to the common people—for all of these roles there have been capable men. Thus, our dynasty's recruitment of talent through the examination system has surpassed that of former eras.

I humbly reflect that His Majesty the Emperor, endowed with the natural gifts for great achievements, has exalted the enterprise of dynastic revival and brought about an era of grand peace. Having expanded the provincial examination quotas, he has also personally performed the ceremony of inspecting the Imperial University; all of this is solely to honor Confucian scholars and revere the Way, to rouse and foster worthy talents so that they may be of service to the state. For scholars who encounter such a time and ascend to such glorious good fortune, how could they not exert themselves in meritorious service so as to repay and match this favor?

Now they have been entered into the registers of the heavenly treasury and will advance to reply to the Emperor in the great court; the day when they will take up official governance and rise to illustrious prominence is at hand. May they strive earnestly, so that the efficacy of Confucian scholars is not merely entrusted to empty words, but is assuredly made manifest throughout the empire…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
後世則人將指而稱之曰此
龍飛第一科進士也不其偉歟苟
徒弄筆墨以徼利達是非
朝廷興賢之意而亦非淵之所
望也於是選次其文為會試
錄遂書以勗之
嘉議大夫戶部右侍郎兼翰
===
林院學士江淵謹序
alt_text:
後世則人將指而稱之曰此
龍飛第一科進士也不其偉歟苟
徒弄筆墨以徼利達是非
朝廷興賢之意而亦非淵之所
望也於是選次其文爲會試
錄遂書以勗之
嘉議大夫戶部右侍郎兼翰
林院學士江淵謹序
punctuated:
後世，則人將指而稱之曰：「此龍飛第一科進士也。」不其偉歟！苟徒弄筆墨以徼利達，是非朝廷興賢之意，而亦非淵之所望也。於是選次其文為《會試錄》，遂書以勗之。
嘉議大夫、戶部右侍郎兼翰林院學士江淵謹序。
translation_en:
…and to posterity, then people will point to them and praise them, saying, "These are the metropolitan graduates (jinshi) of the very first examination following the Emperor's ascension to the throne!" Would that not be magnificent! If, however, they merely play with brush and ink to seek profit and advancement, this is neither the Court's intention in promoting the worthy, nor is it what I, Yuan, hope for. Therefore, having selected and arranged their essays into the Record of the Metropolitan Examination (Huishi lu), I write this to exhort them.
Respectfully prefaced by Jiang Yuan 江淵, Grand Master for Splendid Discussion, Right Vice Minister of Revenue, concurrently Hanlin Academician.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰麻冕禮也今也純儉吾從衆拜下禮
也今拜乎上泰也雖違衆吾從下
百世以俟聖人而不惑知人也是故君子
動而世爲天下道行而世爲天下法
言而世爲天下則遠之則有望近之
則不厭
夫徐行者豈人所不能哉所不爲也堯舜
===
之道孝弟而已矣
易
利有攸往上合志也
明出地上順而麗乎大明柔進而上行是
以康侯用錫馬蕃庶晝日三接也
夫茅之爲物薄而用可重也慎斯術也以
往其无所失矣
爻象動乎内吉凶見乎外功業見乎變聖
人之情見乎辭

第壹場

則不厭
夫徐行者豈人所不能哉所不爲也堯舜
之道孝弟而已矣
===
易
利有攸往上合志也
明出地上順而麗乎大明柔進而上行是
以康侯用錫馬蕃庶晝日三接也
夫茅之爲物薄而用可重也慎斯術也以
往其无所失矣
爻象動乎內吉凶見乎外功業見乎變聖
人之情見乎辭
punctuated:
第壹場

四書
子曰：「麻冕，禮也；今也純，儉，吾從衆。拜下，禮也；今拜乎上，泰也。雖違衆，吾從下。」
百世以俟聖人而不惑，知人也。是故君子動而世爲天下道，行而世爲天下法，言而世爲天下則。遠之則有望，近之則不厭。
夫徐行者，豈人所不能哉？所不爲也。堯舜之道，孝弟而已矣。

易
利有攸往，上合志也。
明出地上，順而麗乎大明，柔進而上行，是以康侯用錫馬蕃庶，晝日三接也。
夫茅之爲物薄，而用可重也。慎斯術也以往，其无所失矣。
爻象動乎内，吉凶見乎外，功業見乎變，聖人之情見乎辭。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books (Sishu)
The Master said: "A linen ceremonial cap is prescribed by the rites, whereas nowadays silk is used; this is frugal, so I follow the majority. Bowing below the hall is prescribed by the rites, whereas nowadays people bow after ascending; this is arrogant. Though it goes against the majority, I follow the practice of bowing below."
To wait a hundred generations for a sage and have no doubts implies knowing men. Therefore, for generations the gentleman's movements serve as the way of the world, for generations his conduct serves as the model of the world, and for generations his words serve as the standard of the world. Those who are far from him look up to him with hope, and those who are near him never weary of him.
Now, walking slowly—is it really something that people are unable to do? It is simply something they do not do. The way of Yao and Shun is nothing more than filial piety and fraternal respect.

Book of Changes (Yi)
"It is advantageous to have somewhere to go": the superior shares the same purpose.
Brightness rises above the earth; devotion clings to great brightness, and the yielding advances and moves upward. Therefore the Marquis of Peace is granted horses in great number and is received in audience three times in a single day.
Now white cogon grass is a trifling thing, yet its use can be of great weight. If one goes forward cautiously with this method, one will suffer no loss.
The lines and images move within, good fortune and misfortune are manifested without, achievements and enterprises are revealed in changes, and the sentiments of the sages are seen in the appended judgements.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
書
織皮崑崙析支渠搜西戎即叙
惟文王之敬忌乃裕民曰我惟有及則予
一人以懌王曰封爽惟民迪吉康我
時其惟殷先哲王德用康乂民作求
予旦以多子越御事篤前人成烈荅其師
作周孚先
尚胥暨顧綏爾先公之臣服于先王雖爾
身在外乃心罔不在王室
===
詩
二之日鑿冰冲冲三之日納于凌陰四之
日其蚤獻羔祭韭九月肅霜十月滌
場朋酒斯饗曰殺羔羊躋彼公堂稱
彼兕觥萬壽無疆
方叔元老克壯其猶方叔率止執訊獲醜
戎車嘽嘽嘽嘽焞焞如霆如雷顯允
方叔征伐玁狁蠻荆来威
作召公考天子萬壽

punctuated:
書
織皮崑崙、析支、渠搜，西戎即叙。
惟文王之敬忌，乃裕民，曰：「我惟有及，則予一人以懌。」王曰：「封，爽惟民，迪吉康。我時其惟殷先哲王德，用康乂民作求。」
予旦以多子越御事，篤前人成烈，荅其師，作周孚先。
尚胥暨顧，綏爾先公之臣服于先王。雖爾身在外，乃心罔不在王室。

詩
二之日鑿冰冲冲，三之日納于凌陰。四之日其蚤，獻羔祭韭。九月肅霜，十月滌場。朋酒斯饗，曰殺羔羊。躋彼公堂，稱彼兕觥，萬壽無疆。
方叔元老，克壯其猶。方叔率止，執訊獲醜。戎車嘽嘽，嘽嘽焞焞，如霆如雷。顯允方叔，征伐玁狁，蠻荆来威。
作召公考，天子萬壽。
translation_en:
Book of Documents (Shu):

 Hair-cloth and skins were brought from Kunlun, Xizhi, and Qusou; the Western Rong all came to order.

"Consider the reverence and caution of King Wen, whereby he enriched the people, saying, 'If only I can attain to this, then I, the One Man, shall be pleased.'" The King said, "Feng, clearly consider the people, and guide them to felicity and peace. I constantly think of the virtue of the former wise kings of Yin, whereby to pacify and govern the people, actively seeking to match them."

"I, Dan, with the numerous nobles and managers of affairs, will consolidate the accomplished achievements of our predecessors, respond to the multitudes, and make Zhou the exemplar of trust."

"May you mutually look after and support one another, and serenely continue the submission of your former dukes to the former kings. Although your person is outside at court's distance, let there be no moment when your heart is not in the royal house."

Book of Odes (Shi):

"In the days of the second month, they hew out the ice with ringing blows; in the days of the third month, they convey it to the ice-house. In the days of the fourth month, early in the morning, they offer a lamb and sacrifice with scallions. In the ninth month, there is biting frost; in the tenth month, they sweep clean the threshing-floor. With twin vessels of wine they hold the feast, and say, 'Let us kill a lamb and a sheep.' They ascend that public hall, raise that rhinoceros-horn goblet, and wish: 'Myriad years of life without end!'"

"Fang Shu, the senior statesman, was strong in his plans. Fang Shu led his forces on, seizing prisoners for questioning and capturing the enemy crowd. His war chariots were numerous—numerous and grand, like crashing thunder and rolling peals. Illustrious and trusty was Fang Shu; he went on expeditions against the Xianyun, and the Man of Jing came in awe of his majesty."

"Make complete the achievement of the Duke of Shao; may the Son of Heaven live for ten thousand years!"

translation_en:
"Now he progresses through the states; may vast Heaven cherish him as its son! Truly Heaven aids and orders the House of Zhou: when he makes a slight move to awe them, there are none who do not tremble in awe. He conciliates and appeases all the spirits, even to the Yellow River and the lofty peaks. Truly the king is the sovereign! Bright and illustrious is the House of Zhou; he orders the nobles in their ranks according to rule. Then he gathers in the shields and halberds, and cases the bows and arrows. 'I seek for admirable virtue, to spread it throughout these great Xia lands; truly I, the king, will preserve it.'"

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The Marquis of Qi sent his younger brother Nian to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" (7th year of Duke Yin). "The Earl of Zheng sent Yuan to come and yield Beng" (8th year of Duke Yin). "Men of Song and men of Wei entered Zheng" (10th year of Duke Yin). "The Duke, together with the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng, entered Xu" (11th year of Duke Yin). "Men of Chu attacked Zheng" (9th year of Duke Wen). "The Viscount of Chu sent Jiao to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" (9th year of Duke Wen). "The Earl of Qin sent Shu to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" (12th year of Duke Wen). "The Duke met with the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Earl of Cao, and Zhao Dun of Jin; on the guiyou day, they covenanted together at Xincheng" (14th year of Duke Wen).

"The King's man Zitu rescued Wei" (6th year of Duke Zhuang). "Yang Chufu of Jin led an army to attack Chu in order to rescue Jiang" (3rd year of Duke Wen).

"The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Zheng met at Juan" (15th year of Duke Zhuang). "The Duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and covenanted together at You"…

translation_en:
Mindfully evaluating the sequence of relative gravity and carefully gauging the measure of depth in order to distinguish them; exhausting one's acute hearing and clear sight, and extending one's loyalty and love to the utmost in order to fulfill them.
These six things are the sounds of virtuous music. Only afterward are bells, chimes, mouth organs, and zithers used to harmonize them, and shields, battle-axes, ox-tail pennants, and pheasant plumes used to dance to them.
Kindness and goodness [慈善, for 慈養?] do not depart from the person, ears and eyes do not depart from the mind, and thoughts and concerns do not depart from the parents; they are bound within the heart, manifested in the countenance, and examined methodically.
Once the five principles have been applied, the sage therefore wears them.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
典謨訓誥之所同者可指而言之歟一
書之間弘綱大旨各有所左亦可舉其
要而悉論之歟孝順事實所載者惟孝
之一事豈能孝亦可以該五者之倫理
歟抑別有其說歟諸士子服膺
聖訓有素其詳著于篇以觀所學
問致治之道莫先於知人薦舉以堯舜之
聖不能無資於僉岳驩兜之薦堯之棄
共工不用是矣乃復用鯀何也故皐陶
===
有知人之謨禹有其難之語是知唐虞
君臣猶以知人為難也若漢唐之君臣
何敢望唐虞其知人乃若有可取者武
帝愛相如之文藻明皇愛李白之英邁
然不過使之從獵任以待詔而已孔明
不許魏延以軍師房喬不許李緯以尚
書四子之浮淺果不足用何知之明歟

…Wherein they correspond with the Canons, Counsels, Instructions, and Announcements [of the Book of Documents]—can these points be specifically identified and discussed? Within each work, the overarching framework and central purport each have their own emphasis [? 左, likely for 在 or 主]; can you also cite their essentials and discuss them in full? What is recorded in the Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) concerns only the single matter of filial piety; is it that being filial can also encompass all five moral relationships? Or is there another explanation? You gentlemen have long cherished the Sacred Instructions in your hearts; set forth your views in detail in your essays, so that we may observe what you have learned.

Question: In the way of achieving good governance, nothing takes precedence over knowing men and recommending them for office. Even with the sageliness of Yao and Shun, they could not do without relying on the assembled ministers and the Four Peaks. When Huandou recommended Gonggong, Yao rejected him and did not employ him, which was right; yet he went on to employ Gun—why was this? Thus Gaoyao offered his counsel on knowing men, and Yu spoke the words "that is difficult," from which we know that even the rulers and ministers of Tang and Yu regarded knowing men as difficult. As for the rulers and ministers of the Han and Tang, how could they dare hope to match Tang and Yu? Yet in their knowing of men, there seems to be something worthy of note: Emperor Wu [of Han] loved the literary brilliance of [Sima] Xiangru, and Emperor Minghuang [Xuanzong of Tang] loved the heroic spirit of Li Bai, yet they did no more than have them attend imperial hunts or appoint them as Expectant Officials (daizhao); Kongming [Zhuge Liang] would not grant Wei Yan the role of Army Supervisor (junshi) [or military strategist], and Fang Qiao [Fang Xuanling] would not approve Li Wei as a Minister (shangshu). The superficiality and shallowness of those four men indeed made them unfit for great employment—how clear was such insight into men! Yet when they knew men like this, why were order and disorder nonetheless so inconsistent? Among Song ministers, there were those who recommended men directly from commoner status to become Lecturers-in-Waiting (shijiang) or Recorders (zhubu); did those men's…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
才行果稱所舉歟恭惟
皇上勵精圖治務先得人知人之鑒軼唐虞而
陋漢唐嘗下
明詔舉才德命廷臣廣薦舉而治效未臻何
歟豈所舉非親則故有未當歟抑奔競
僥倖者多不足以副任使歟抑知之未
精靜言庸違者反誤進而廉退方正者
乃不及舉歟抑別有其故歟伊欲廟堂
之上舉得正人君子有資唐虞之治無
===

其說
問大學論孟中庸四書者孔門聖賢相傳

才行，果稱所舉歟？恭惟皇上勵精圖治，務先得人，知人之鑒，軼唐虞而陋漢唐。嘗下明詔舉才德，命廷臣廣薦舉，而治效未臻，何歟？豈所舉非親則故，有未當歟？抑奔競僥倖者多，不足以副任使歟？抑知之未精，靜言庸違者反誤進，而廉退方正者乃不及舉歟？抑別有其故歟？伊欲廟堂之上，舉得正人君子，有資唐虞之治，無愧禹、皐陶之言者，果何以致之歟？必有其說。

問：《大學》、《論》、《孟》、《中庸》四書者，孔門聖賢相傳之心法，固學者所當講也。今即其書論之，先儒以為《大學》始終不出乎敬，《中庸》之樞紐不出乎誠，《論語》之要在於操存涵養，《孟子》之要在於體驗充廣。其必各有所指也，可得而言其槩歟？四書之學，莫先於修身。《論語》言修身曰「修己以敬」，
translation_en:
…talents and conduct truly match the recommendations made for them?

Reverently we reflect that His Majesty works tirelessly for good governance, making the acquisition of capable men his first priority; his insight in knowing men surpasses that of Tang and Yu [Yao and Shun] and makes Han and Tang look paltry. He has previously issued clear edicts calling for the recommendation of men of talent and virtue, ordering court officials to make broad nominations, and yet the full efficacy of governance has not been achieved—why is this? Could it be that those recommended are either relatives or old acquaintances, and therefore not suitable? Or that there are too many who scramble for advancement and seek luck, who are inadequate to fulfill the responsibilities entrusted to them? Or that the discernment of men is not yet precise, so that those who speak smoothly when idle but act perversely when employed are mistakenly promoted instead, while the incorrupt, retiring, and upright fail to be recommended? Or is there some other reason? If we wish for those in the court above to recommend upright men and gentlemen who can contribute to a governance like that of Tang and Yu and not put to shame the words of Yu and Gao Yao, how indeed is this to be brought about? There must be an explanation for this.

Question: The Four Books—the Great Learning (Daxue), the Analects (Lunyu), the Mencius (Mengzi), and the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong)—embody the method of the mind-and-heart transmitted by the sages and worthies of the Confucian school, which scholars certainly ought to study and discuss. Now, examining them directly on the basis of the texts themselves, former Confucians held that from beginning to end the Great Learning does not go beyond reverence (jing), that the pivot of the Doctrine of the Mean does not go beyond sincerity (cheng), that the essential point of the Analects lies in preserving the mind and nurturing one's nature, and that the essential point of the Mencius lies in personal realization and extension. Each of these statements must have its specific referent; can you state their general import? In the learning of the Four Books, nothing comes before cultivating the person. In speaking of cultivating the person, the Analects says, "Cultivate oneself with reverence";…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
中庸曰修身以道大學則曰心正而后
身修修身一也曰敬曰道曰正心其言
之不同何歟修身而後治人論語言治
人曰修己以安百姓大學曰國治而后
天下平中庸曰君子篤恭而天下平而
孟子則曰人人親其親長其長而天下
平其言之不一何歟夫學有其要而治
出一本今欲盡修身之道將從事於敬
與道而又正心歟抑固自有先後之序
===
得其一可該其餘歟盡治人之道將但
修身與篤恭而已乎抑猶不免治國及
使人親親長長歟修治之道固所當先
聖賢之言宜無不同諸士子窮經問學
有年必講之熟矣幸相與言之
問科目之設自隋唐以來專試文藝盖以
文足以明理理明足以致諸用也我
朝重進士之科其所以選之精待之厚者盖
將望其奮忠義如昔之出入將相收功

《中庸》曰「修身以道」，《大學》則曰「心正而后身修」。修身一也，曰敬、曰道、曰正心，其言之不同，何歟？修身而後治人，《論語》言治人曰「修己以安百姓」，《大學》曰「國治而后天下平」，《中庸》曰「君子篤恭而天下平」，而《孟子》則曰「人人親其親，長其長，而天下平」。其言之不一，何歟？夫學有其要，而治出一本。今欲盡修身之道，將從事於敬與道而又正心歟？抑固自有先後之序，得其一可該其餘歟？盡治人之道，將但修身與篤恭而已乎？抑猶不免治國及使人親親、長長歟？修治之道，固所當先，聖賢之言，宜無不同。諸士子窮經問學有年，必講之熟矣，幸相與言之。

問：科目之設，自隋、唐以來，專試文藝，盖以文足以明理，理明足以致諸用也。我朝重進士之科，其所以選之精、待之厚者，盖將望其奮忠義，如昔之出入將相、收功
translation_en:
… the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) says "cultivate the person by means of the Way," while the Great Learning (Daxue) says "only when the mind is rectified is the person cultivated." Cultivating the person is one and the same thing; why then do their words differ in speaking of reverence, of the Way, and of rectifying the mind? Only after cultivating the person does one govern others. In speaking of governing others, the Analects (Lunyu) says "cultivate oneself in order to give peace to the hundred surnames"; the Great Learning says "only when the state is rightly governed is the world at peace"; the Doctrine of the Mean says "the superior man is earnestly reverent and the world is at peace"; whereas Mencius (Mengzi) says "when everyone loves his parents and respects his elders, the world is at peace." Why are their words not uniform? Now learning has its essentials, and governance issues from a single root. If today one wishes to exhaust the Way of cultivating the person, shall one engage in reverence and the Way and also rectify the mind? Or is there inherently an order of precedence among them, such that attaining one can encompass the rest? And to exhaust the Way of governing others, shall one merely cultivate the person and be earnestly reverent and nothing more? Or must one still not avoid governing the state and causing people to love their parents and respect their elders? The Way of self-cultivation and governance is assuredly what must come first, and the words of the sages and worthies ought not to differ. You gentlemen have thoroughly studied the Classics and pursued learning for years, and have surely discussed these matters until you are familiar with them; pray set forth your views together.

Our dynasty attaches great importance to the category of metropolitan graduates (jinshi). The reason it selects them with such refinement and treats them with such generosity is that it hopes they will rouse themselves to loyalty and righteousness, like one of old who went out as general and came in as chief minister, achieving merit in …

translation_en:
… Huai and Cai, yet why is it that today there are not a few who shrink back when encountering affairs? It hopes they will offer loyal and forthright counsel like the man of old who gathered and arranged instances of success and failure into fifty categories, yet why do those today who harbor deceit and practice flattery follow upon one another's heels? It hopes they will maintain incorruptible integrity like the man of old who, when presented with a million cash, refused to accept it so as to avoid wasteful expenditure, yet why are those today who greedily seek gain insatiable? It hopes they will practice quiet retirement like the men of old who declined to take the Palace Examination because their fathers held posts as chief councilors, yet why are those today who engage in illicit solicitation seen everywhere? It hopes they will promote what is beneficial and eliminate what is harmful like the man of old who tamed the crocodiles, yet why do those today who sit by and watch the people's sufferings stand shoulder to shoulder? Men of the past have said that the metropolitan graduate (jinshi) examination is insufficient for obtaining capable men; looking at it from today's perspective, is this truly so? Yet all the aforementioned worthies emerged from this very path. Could it be that men of the present cannot match those of the past? Or is it that our selection has not yet achieved refinement? Or is there some other reason? You scholars have come by way of the examination categories, and your aspirations are surely already formed. If we wish to obtain men like those worthies of the past, so as to fulfill the Court's intention in selecting scholars, there must be a way to do so. Please speak of it in detail.

punctuated: 賤而疎，不以罪而棄。古人有舉自射鈎、拔於寒微，或以怯懦、或以人奴，或不親戎服、不便鞍馬，或用於罪累、收於降附，卒能建立大勳，助成伯王之業者，其人可得聞歟？凡選將以五才為體，五謹為用，又考之以九驗之言詞，復之以九術之科例，其法可詳知歟？然將之伎能、局力不齊，有所謂十、百、千、萬人之將，十萬、百萬人之將者，果何所試而知其才器高下以任使之歟？又有五危、十過者，將之害也，可詳知歟？今國家方注意選將，盖有其人矣。伊欲其克敵制勝，皆如古之名將，迅掃千里，以痛快人心，果何以致之歟？抑别有道以激勸之歟？幸詳言之，毋隱。
translation_en: …alienating them because of low station, nor discarding them because of past offenses. Among the ancients, there were those raised up after shooting a belt-hook or elevated from humble obscurity; some were once known for timidity, or had been slaves; some did not wear military attire in person or were unaccustomed to saddle and horse; some were employed while entangled in guilt, or taken in from among the surrendered and newly submitted—yet in the end they were able to establish great merit and help accomplish the enterprise of hegemons and true kings. May we hear who those men were? In general, in selecting generals one takes the "five talents" (wucai) as the substance and the "five cautions" (wujin) as the function, and further examines them through the words of the "nine verifications" (jiuyan) and tests them against the categories of the "nine methods" (jiushu). Can these methods be known in detail? Yet the skills and capacities of generals are not uniform: there are those called generals of ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand men, and generals of a hundred thousand or a million men. By what tests, indeed, does one know the relative grade of their talent and capacity so as to commission and employ them accordingly? Furthermore, there are the "five dangers" (wuwei) and the "ten faults" (shiguo), which are thebanes of a general. Can these be known in detail? At present, the State is focusing its attention on selecting generals, and indeed such men exist. If we wish them to vanquish the enemy and secure victory, all like the famous generals of antiquity, swiftly sweeping clear a thousand li to the great satisfaction of people's hearts, how is this in fact to be brought about? Or is there some other way to rouse and encourage them? Please set this forth in detail and hold nothing back.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
四書
百世以俟聖人而不惑知人也是故君子動而
世為天下道行而世為天下法言而世為天下
則遠之則有望近之則不厭
吳福
同考試官主事錢批此題頭緒似多不過俟後聖
徵諸庶民要終原始之意作者多輕重詳畧
失倫不能歸一此篇獨能得之一結尤佳
同考試官修撰李批此題作者多以功效言分
===
截不明甚失本旨此篇於俟後聖徵諸庶民
處說理明白足見本領之學
考試官修撰林批理明白而詞簡當蓋精於中庸
之學者
考試官學士江批詞理明健優出衆作可取
中庸論君子之道既推夫驗諸後聖之由復申夫徵
諸庶民之實蓋知人者驗諸後聖之由而言行法則
於天下後世而無間者徵諸庶民之實也大賢要終
原始而言之其明人道之意深矣今夫王天下之君

Four Books

"Wait a hundred generations for a sage and have no doubts: this is to know men. Therefore, for a gentleman, his movements for generations are a path for the world, his actions for generations are a model for the world, and his words for generations are a standard for the world. Those who are far from him look up to him; those who are near him do not tire of him."

text:
于行三重之事惟其本諸身者有其德故其驗於外
者無不合以言其驗於遠也百世之相去若此其懸
絕後聖之未至若此其難料而吾之所行可以俟之
而不惑焉其所以不惑者初非讖緯術數也以其知
人焉耳蓋人者理之所寓而聖人者人道之極也聖
人盡人道之極而明人理之至以之而俟後聖所謂
聖人復起不易吾言矣夫何有於惑乎此其遠有以
驗乎近者如此以言其徵諸庶民也君子惟其無動
動則世為天下道焉動兼言行而言道兼法則而言
===

也動形於言則言為天下後世之準則而人所取正
也地之遠者悅其德之廣被而有企慕之心地之近
者習其行之有常而無厭斁之意此其下有以驗乎
上者如此中庸論君子之道無往不合至是而無以
加矣抑論之君子之道必本諸身而後可以徵諸民
徵諸民而後可以考三王建天地質鬼神而俟後聖
也蓋不徵諸民則民且不從何以驗諸幽明先後乎

…[gentleman], in carrying out the three weighty matters, simply because what is rooted in his own person possesses the requisite virtue, when it is verified externally nothing fails to accord.

To speak of its verification in the distant future: a hundred generations are separated by so vast a gulf, and the arrival of a future sage is so difficult to foresee, yet what I practice can await him without doubt. The reason one has no doubt is by no means due to prognostic apocrypha or calculative arts; it is simply because one knows men. For man is that in which principle resides, and the sage is the ultimate standard of the human way. When a sage exhausts the ultimate standard of the human way and illuminates the utmost of human principle, awaiting a future sage on this basis is what is meant by "Even if a sage were to arise again, he would not change my words"—what doubt could there possibly be? Such is the way in which the distant verifies the near.

To speak of its attestation among the common people: as long as the gentleman does not act, that is all; when he acts, for generations it becomes a universal way for the world. "Action" encompasses both words and deeds, while "way" encompasses both law and model. For when action takes form in deeds, his deeds become the law for the world and future generations, which people ought to observe; when action takes form in words, his words become the standard for the world and future generations, by which people rectify themselves. Those in distant lands delight in the wide reach of his virtue and harbor feelings of eager admiration; those in nearby lands grow accustomed to the constancy of his conduct and have no thought of weariness. Such is the way in which those below verify those above.

The discussion in the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) of how the Way of the gentleman accords in every respect reaches its culmination here and nothing further can be added. Yet if we consider it further, the Way of the gentleman must first be rooted in his own person before it can be attested by the people, and only after it is attested by the people can it be tested against the Three Kings, established before heaven and earth, confirmed before ghosts and spirits, and await a future sage. For if it is not attested by the people, the people will not even follow him—how then could it be verified across the unseen and the manifest, or across past and future? And if it is not rooted in his own person, his person is not even cultivated—how then could he bring the people to follow him? Master Zisi, in…

One's natural disposition is not something difficult for men to practice, and the Way of the Sages is nothing outside of this nature. Now filial piety and fraternal respect belong to one's natural disposition; as men's innate knowledge and innate ability, there is nothing about them that is difficult to practice. Even though the Sages represent the ultimate perfection of human relationships, they merely follow this nature and nothing more—how could they add even a hair's breadth to it? In the past, when Mencius instructed Cao Jiao 曹交, he spoke to this effect: "Walking slowly behind one's elders is called fraternal respect; walking quickly ahead of one's elders is called a lack of fraternal respect." Now walking slowly behind one's elders is the way of fraternal respect. This way is rooted in what is inherently present in the human mind; it is not something exceedingly hidden and difficult to know—how could it be something one is incapable of? It is only that men themselves cast it aside and do not follow it. This way is closely tied to the constant practices of daily life; it is not something exceedingly lofty and difficult to practice—how could it be something one is incapable of? It is only that men themselves neglect it and do not practice …

translation_en:
…to put it into practice. If one extends and enlarges this nature, the Way of Yao and Shun is right here within it. Now, Yao's being a sage was the ultimate perfection of the Way of Man; yet the reason he was the ultimate perfection of the Way of Man was simply that he followed this nature to fulfill the way of love and respect—how could anything have been added to it? Shun's being a sage was the culmination of human relationships; yet the reason he was the culmination of human relationships was likewise simply that he followed this nature to fulfill the way of serving parents and elders—how could anything have been augmented to it? Therefore, when I say that "one's natural nature is not something difficult for people to practice, and the Way of the sages does not lie outside this nature," this is what I mean. Furthermore, if we examine Cao Jiao's audience with Mencius, he immediately asked whether "all men may become Yao and Shun," and even compared his own physical stature to that of Tang. Mencius first illustrated the point with the example of Wu Huo, and then repeatedly used the filial and fraternal words and deeds of Yao and Shun to encourage him to advance. Alas, Cao Jiao had not yet attained the proper ritual propriety in serving his elders, and his mind was not earnest in seeking the Way. Thus, Mencius taught him filial piety and fraternal duty while refusing to accept him as a disciple. This was in the spirit of Confucius's teaching of "using one's spare energy to study polite letters," and was it not also a form of "teaching by refusing to teach"?

Classic of Changes (Yi)

同宜乎有所進而无不獲也嘗觀大畜之卦合艮乾
二體而成以艮畜乾畜之大者也爻至九三周公既

九同志爾上九有陽剛之才三則合之而不牽於陰

When the Sage explained the line statement's prognostication that it is advantageous to advance, he necesariamente deduced its meaning from sharing the same purpose with the line above, for only when purposes are shared can one make an advance. In the Daxu ("Great Taming") hexagram, Nine in the Third Place corresponds with Nine at the Top and shares the same purpose; it is fitting indeed that it makes an advance and fails to attain nothing. If we examine the Daxu hexagram, it is formed by combining the two trigrams Gen and Qian; using Gen to tame Qian is taming on a great scale. When the lines reach Nine in the Third Place, the Duke of Zhou already spoke of it in the words: "Pursuing with fine horses; it is advantageous to be resolute amidst difficulty. Daily practicing with chariot and defense, it is advantageous to have somewhere to go." When our Master [Confucius] wrote the Commentaries on the Changes, why did he elaborate on this by saying, "'It is advantageous to have somewhere to go': the one above shares the same purpose"? He meant that the line Nine in the Third Place, as a yang line occupying the culmination of strength [the trigram Qian], is no longer restrained and desires to advance upward. Seeing that its advance is not a mere advance, when it advances it achieves what is proper—unlike the First line, which "faces danger, and finds it advantageous to desist," being stopped by Six in the Fourth Place. Its going is not a mere going, and in going there is nothing disadvantageous—unlike the Second line, whose "chariot loses its axle-straps," being restrained by Six in the Fifth Place. That Nine in the Third Place finds it "advantageous to have somewhere to go" is due to nothing other than its sharing the same purpose with Nine at the Top. Nine at the Top possesses yang-firm talent, and the Third line joins with it without being dragged back by yin-softness; Nine at the Top attains the smooth success of the "highway of Heaven," and the Third line accords with it without lingering in bogged-down delay. While this line advantageously advances and harmonizes with the Top, that line carries out its way on a grand scale and does not differ from the Third. Above and below are of one mind and advance together; that side and this share the same aspiration and go forth in company. How could this be compared to the Fourth line's "head-board on a young bull" toward the First, or the Fifth line's "gelded boar" toward the Second, where they do not harmonize with each other? Could the superior man of Nine in the Third Place finding it "advantageous to have somewhere to go" be without a source? Furthermore, among the six lines of this hexagram, the upper trigram is Gen, which is the one that restrains; the lower trigram is Qian, which is the one subjected to restraint. 之象為地悔離之象為日以離日之明而出於坤地
之上非明出地上乎以徳言之離之徳為明坤之徳

然其變又自觀之六四進而居五則是柔進而上行

translation_en: …when the later sage explained it, how could he not fully enumerate its meanings to show that the diviner, possessing such goodness, receives such favor? Consider how the hexagram Jin (Progress) combines the trigrams Kun and Li to form its body. Speaking in terms of its images (xiang), the image of the lower trigram (zhen) Kun is earth, and the image of the upper trigram (hui) Li is the sun. With the brightness of the sun of Li rising above the earth of Kun, is this not "brightness rising above the earth"? Speaking in terms of its virtues (de), the virtue of Li is brightness, and the virtue of Kun is docility. With the docility of Kun attached below the brightness of Li, is this not "being docile and adhering to great brightness"? Moreover, its transformation (bian) comes from the six in the fourth place of the hexagram Guan advancing to occupy the fifth place; this is "the yielding advancing and moving upward." Now, having the form of a ruler of men through the brightness of Li, and advancing through gentleness, means the ruler is bright yet capable of gentleness; having the image of supporting the king through the docility of Kun, and sharing the same virtue with the one above, means the minister is docile and achieves merit. As bright advancement grows ever more flourishing, ruler and minister meet right at the proper time. Thus we see the minister docile below, able to fulfill the duties of bringing peace and order, and the ruler bright above, conferring ever greater ceremonial courtesies upon the "peace-bringing marquis" (kanghou). Thereupon, bestowing horses upon him will surely reach the multitude of ten or a hundred teams of four; receiving him in daytime audiences will reach the glory of a second and a third reception. How great, then, is his receiving of abundant gifts and his being illustriously favored with intimate courtesies! The sage used the hexagram's images, virtues, and transformation to explain the goodness of the hexagram statement, showing that a diviner who possesses such goodness ought likewise to obtain such favor. Even so, because of the goodness of the hexagram statement, the diviner is fittingly assured of good fortune; yet if we seek among the ancients for someone able to match this, who might it be? The Duke of Zhou assisted as prime minister and pacified Zhou, and so received the enfeoffment of a thousand chariots in the state of Lu—how could that merely be compared to "bestowing horses in multitude"? Duke Wen of Jin repelled the barbarians and honored Zhou, and so received the favor of three audiences going in and out—coming close to the utmost intimate courtesy of "three receptions." text:

This is why King Wu, in instructing Kangshu, expressed his meaning in both respects. Moreover, his meaning was as if to say: When Kangshu, as ruler of a feudal state, pacifies the newly established state of Wei, how could he seek it anywhere else? He need only emulate King Wen's reverence and caution. Being reverent, there are things one does not neglect; being cautious, there are things one does not dare to do. What is called reverence and what is called caution is King Wen's mind of being careful with punishments. If Kangshu can emulate King Wen's reverence and caution, then he can hope for King Wen's achievements. From this, he expected him to enrich his people, saying: Under King Wen's model, transforming influence spread along the Jiang and Han rivers; now in your enriching the people, you must share in that same transforming influence without fail [?]. If it is like this, then the ruler will rejoice above, the people will rely on you below, and will not the mind of me, the One Man, be at peace and delighted [?]? By means of this, King Wu held Kangshu to strict standards; his expectations for him may be said to have been deep [?]. Yet in his mind he especially considered that rather than applying punishments with reverence and caution, how much better it would be to guide the people toward auspicious tranquility! Thereupon he again called Kangshu by name and instructed him, meaning that he should clearly reflect upon the people and personally guide them into auspicious tranquility. Benevolence, righteousness, filial piety, and respect are that whereby the people attain auspicious tranquility. Guiding them with benevolence and righteousness so that the people themselves become benevolent and righteous, and guiding them with filial piety and respect so that the people themselves become filial and respectful—this is the very means of leading them into auspicious tranquility. Among the ancients there was one who practiced this. Able to be寬 (magnanimous) and able to be benevolent, Tang once used this virtue to manifest trust among the people; how could I not use tranquility to protect the people, and think of matching his fine virtue? text:

…may be said to have reached the utmost. Alas! The stations of ruler and minister are different, yet they share the same strict reverence; the words of their strict reverence are different, yet they share the same emulation of the former sages. This being so, the earlier strict reverence was certainly meant to encourage Kangshu, and the later strict reverence was likewise meant to encourage Kangshu—how heavy indeed was Kangshu's responsibility! Furthermore, if we examine the "Announcement to the Prince of Kang" (Kang gao) as a whole, it takes making bright one's virtue and being cautious in punishments as its guiding principle. Thus, it desires both that he make bright his virtue and that he be cautious in punishments; it desires both that he apply punishments through virtue and that he employ virtue rather than punishments. That from beginning to end it speaks entirely in terms of virtue shows how profound was the intention conveyed to Kangshu!

Comment by Associate Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Liu: This topic is inherently straightforward, yet writers frequently divide the passage into sections after "consolidate the achievements of our predecessors," which quite misses the meaning of the Classic. This paper alone is clear and fluent in its reasoning and style; written no doubt by someone well-versed in the Classic, it ought to be placed in the front ranks.

text:
大臣率屬以治洛在乎厚前人之功以慰其民盡事
君之道以倡其後盖前人之功固賴後人継之而後
人事君之道尤賴前人倡之二者兼盡惟周公乎昔
周公以治洛之事自效其意若曰修和有夏萬邦作
孚此文王之成烈而天下之所仰望者也今予以衆
卿大夫及治事之臣篤厚之而使益顯則所謂覲文
王之耿光者在是寧不有以慰天下仰望之心乎燮
伐大商會朝清明此武王之成烈而天下之所企慕
者也今予以衆卿大夫及治事之臣篤厚之而使益
===
著則所謂揚武王之大烈者在是寧不有以荅天下
企慕之心乎況夫臨鎮之初政教攸始百僚之視效
在焉故凡攄忠效誠而無一毫之或欺者雖信以事
上也抑亦以倡夫後之事上者莫不信焉殫力竭心
而無一毫之不實者雖信以輔君也抑亦以倡夫後
之輔君者亦莫不信焉吁周公以是為言其自任之
重為何如哉抑考周公上文以治洛之效責之成王
則曰作周恭先於此治洛之事任諸巳則曰作周

translation_en:
For a great minister to lead his subordinates in governing Luo lies in consolidating the achievements of his predecessors so as to comfort the people, and fulfilling the Way of serving the ruler so as to lead those who come after. For the achievements of predecessors certainly depend on successors to continue them, while the Way by which successors serve their ruler depends even more on predecessors to initiate it. Was it not the Duke of Zhou alone who fulfilled both of these?

In antiquity, the Duke of Zhou devoted himself to the task of governing Luo, his meaning being as if to say: "Bringing order and harmony to the central states, so that the myriad regions responded with trust"—this was the accomplished merit of King Wen, to which all under heaven looked up in hope. Now if I, together with the various grandees, great officers, and officials in charge of affairs, consolidate this and make it ever more illustrious, then what is called "manifesting the bright glory of King Wen" lies right here; how could this fail to comfort the hopeful hearts of all under heaven? "In harmony striking down great Shang, the morning of the encounter was clear and bright"—this was the accomplished merit of King Wu, which all under heaven eagerly admired. Now if I, together with the various grandees, great officers, and officials in charge of affairs, consolidate this and make it ever more manifest, then what is called "extolling the great merit of King Wu" lies right here; how could this fail to answer the admiring hearts of all under heaven?

Moreover, at the outset of assuming command over the garrison, when governance and moral instruction first begin, the hundred officials look to this as their model. Therefore, in all cases of expressing loyalty and rendering sincerity without the slightest deceit, although one is serving the sovereign in good faith, one is also setting an example so that none who serve the sovereign hereafter will fail to be trustworthy. In exhausting one's strength and devoting one's heart without the slightest insincerity, although one is assisting the ruler in good faith, one is also setting an example so that none who assist the ruler hereafter will fail to be trustworthy either.

Ah! For the Duke of Zhou to speak thus, how weighty was the responsibility he took upon himself! Furthermore, if we examine how in the preceding passage the Duke of Zhou charged King Cheng with the efficacy of governing Luo, saying "be the first in reverence for Zhou," while here in taking the task of governing Luo upon himself, he says "be the first in trustworthiness for Zhou"—the reason is none other than that he wished King Cheng [?] to fulfill the Way of being a ruler as a model for later kings, while I…

Comment by Associate Examiner Administration Vice Commissioner Luo: Our ward had the largest number of examination papers on the Classic of Poetry. On this topic, most candidates took the words prior to the fourth stanza to be the text of the king's commission, which made for tiresome reading. This composition alone points solely to the jade-handled libation ladle and black millet wine, and the bestowal of hills, lands, and fields; furthermore, it depicts Shao Hu's 召虎 sentiments in inscribing the vessels and wishing the ruler longevity so vividly that one feels as if present at the time. It deserves to rank first among the papers on the Classic of Poetry.
Comment by Examiner Senior Compiler Lin: With earnest intent and graceful phrasing, it captures the spirit of mutual rapport between ruler and minister during the Zhou restoration.
Comment by Examiner Academician Jiang: It depicts the great minister's intention in inscribing the vessels and wishing his ruler longevity with subtle thoroughness; the author must be one who has deeply grasped the teaching of gentle and sincere厚 (wenrou dunhou) [poetics].

Inscribing ancestral temple vessels to commemorate one's accomplishment, and wishing the ruler longevity to the utmost duration—such is how a great minister receives his charge. For inscribing the vessels is the means to revere the ruler's command without ever forgetting it, and wishing him longevity is the means to express an unending heart of affection for the ruler. Were he not a great minister of the Zhou restoration, how could he have been capable of this? Of old, King Xuan commanded Duke Mu [of Shao] to pacify the Yi tribes south of the Huai River. When he reported the completion of his meritorious service, the king bestowed upon him a written commission, with a jade-handled libation ladle and black millet wine with which to sacrifice to his ancestors, and mountains, rivers, lands, and fields with which to enlarge his fief. 「時邁其邦，昊天其子之，實右序有周。薄言震之，
translation_en:
… command and felt gratitude for the sovereign's grace; earnestly he made the ancestral temple vessels for Duke Kang, and intently he inscribed the royal patent of investiture upon them. "I bestow upon you a jade libation ladle and a jar of black-millet aromatic wine"—these were the words of the patent of investiture. Duke Mu inscribed them upon goblets and grain tureens to verify that his achievements in defining boundaries and ordering the land were complete, and whether he had indeed brought no shame upon Duke Kang. "Report to your accomplished ancestors, and I grant you mountains, lands, and fields"—these were the words of the patent of investiture. Duke Mu inscribed them upon tripods and ritual vessels to verify that his achievements in going everywhere to promulgate the royal orders were complete, and whether he had indeed no cause to blush before Duke Kang. Once the words of the patent of investiture were inscribed upon the temple vessels, the sincerity of his loyalty and affection immediately took form in prayers and eulogies. Were he to wish his sovereign wealth, his sovereign already possessed the wealth of all within the Four Seas; were he to wish his sovereign noble rank, his sovereign already held the noble rank of Son of Heaven; thus he could only wish his sovereign longevity. And in wishing longevity he necessarily said "a myriad years of life," praying that his sovereign might reach the wizened visage and mottled back of extreme old age, and for ten thousand years forever preserve the wealth of the Four Seas; praying that his sovereign might attain the yellowed hair and renewed teeth of longevity, and for ten thousand and a thousand years forever occupy the exalted fifth-line position of the throne. Ah! In the making of the temple vessels, on the one hand he inscribed the sovereign's command, and on the other he prayed for the sovereign's longevity. Thus not only would the sovereign's command endure as long as the temple vessels, but the sovereign's longevity would also endure as long as the temple vessels. May Duke Mu not be called one skilled in prayers and eulogies! Yet if we examine the verses of this stanza, the first four lines are words of prayer and eulogy, while the last four lines are words of exhortation. Prayer and eulogy are the means to answer the sovereign's bounty; exhortation is the means to advance the sovereign in the Way. Now that the Huai tribes had submitted, the king's fine reputation was already manifest, yet Duke Mu necessarily prayed that his fine reputation would never cease; now that the four quarters were pacified, the king's martial achievements were complete, yet Duke Mu necessarily prayed that his civil virtue would be broadly diffused. Ah! What the ancients called serving the sovereign according to the Way—Duke Mu exemplified it.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
莫不震疊懷柔百神及河喬嶽允王維后明昭
有周式序在位載戢干戈載櫜弓矢我求懿德
肆于時夏允王保之
吳匯
同考試官叅政羅批此題頌武王巡守而朝會祭
告之事首兩句摠言以發端下兩節分言其事連
日閱卷苦無佳者忽得此篇理明辭贍宜置前列
考試官修撰林批詞氣舂容得詩人美盛德之形容
考試官學士江批鋪叙武王巡守朝會祭告之事
===
理明詞贍允宜高薦
王者巡侯國而天眷不敢必既驗天意於人神而信
其君天下復新一代之政教而信其保天命蓋天眷
固不敢必也今也人神交帰政教畢舉則武王所以
君天下而保天命者豈不深可信乎昔武王受命而
為天子以時巡行諸侯之國其意若曰祭告之禮我
所當舉也朝會之禮我所當行也天其子我我不敢
必也天廿其不子我我亦不敢必也天眷雖不敢必而
天意實有可驗尊我於諸侯之上繼我於夏商之後

考試官修撰林批：詞氣舂容，得詩人美盛德之形容。
考試官學士江批：鋪叙武王巡守朝會祭告之事，理明詞贍，允宜高薦。

王者巡侯國，而天眷不敢必；既驗天意於人神而信其君天下，復新一代之政教而信其保天命。蓋天眷固不敢必也，今也人神交帰，政教畢舉，則武王所以君天下而保天命者，豈不深可信乎？昔武王受命而為天子，以時巡行諸侯之國。其意若曰：祭告之禮，我所當舉也；朝會之禮，我所當行也。天其子我，我不敢必也；天廿其不子我，我亦不敢必也。天眷雖不敢必，而天意實有可驗：尊我於諸侯之上，繼我於夏、商之後，
translation_en:
… none do not tremble with awe. He conciliates and comforts the hundred spirits, reaching to the Yellow River and the lofty Sacred Peaks. Truly the king is the sovereign! Brightly illustrious is the House of Zhou; he orders those in office according to their ranks. Now he gathers in the shields and halberds, now he cases the bows and arrows. We seek admirable virtue and spread it throughout this realm of Xia; truly the king will preserve the Mandate."

Wu Hui

Associate Examiner, Administration Vice Commissioner Luo, comments: This topic eulogizes the affairs of King Wu's tour of inspection, holding court audiences and offering sacrificial announcements. The first two lines make a general statement to introduce the theme, while the following two sections separately set forth the affairs. For several consecutive days of reading papers, I suffered from finding no fine ones; suddenly obtaining this essay, whose reasoning is clear and diction rich, it ought to be placed in the front ranks.
Examiner, Senior Compiler Lin, comments: Its tone and phrasing are leisurely and dignified, capturing the poet's depiction in praising flourishing virtue.
Examiner, Academician Jiang, comments: It sets forth at length the affairs of King Wu's tour of inspection, court audiences, and sacrificial announcements; its reasoning is clear and its diction rich, so it truly deserves high recommendation.

When the true king tours the states of the feudal lords, he dares not take Heaven's favor for granted; having verified Heaven's will among men and spirits and thus believed that he is sovereign over the realm, he further renews the governance and moral instruction of a new dynasty and thus believes that he will preserve the Mandate of Heaven. Indeed, Heaven's favor may certainly not be taken for granted. Now, when both men and spirits turn to him in allegiance and governance and instruction are completely instituted, how could that by which King Wu acts as sovereign over the realm and preserves the Mandate of Heaven not be deeply credible? In antiquity, when King Wu received the Mandate and became the Son of Heaven, in due season he toured the states of the feudal lords. His thought was as if to say: "The rites of sacrificial announcement are what I ought to perform; the rites of court audience are what I ought to practice. Whether Heaven treats me as its son, I dare not take for granted; whether Heaven [?] does not treat me as its son, I likewise dare not take for granted." Yet although Heaven's favor could not be taken for granted, Heaven's will could in fact be verified: exalting me above the feudal lords, making me succeed after the Xia and Shang…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
非天實右序我周乎故使我薄言震動於諸侯也大國
之侯伯小國之子男莫不震懼於方嶽之下懷柔百
於百神也深廣之河崇高之嶽莫不感格於祭告之
時則信乎武王之為天下君矣君天下既驗於人神
之帰保天命尤在於政教之舉故又言明昭乎我周
也既以慶讓黜陟之典式序在位之諸侯有功有徳
者則有加地進律之賞不敬不順者則有黜地削爵
之罰彼稱干比戈昔以戡亂者今則戢之而弗試張
弓挾矢昔以伐罪者今則櫜之而弗用父子之親君
===
臣之義懿徳也我則益求之以布于中國以敦教化
長幼之序夫婦之別懿徳也我則益求之以陳于華
夏以厚風俗則信乎武王之能保天命矣吁始焉天
眷不敢必者以見武王敬天之心也終焉天命之保
深可信者以見武王克盡為君之道也詩人其善於
美盛徳之形容者歟抑考之槩亦巡守而作其曰堕
山喬嶽允猶翕河即懷柔百神事也其曰敷天之下
裒時之對即震疊諸侯事也讀者合而觀之則周家
所以得神人之帰者益可驗

裒時之對即震疊諸侯事也讀者合而觀之則周家
所以得神人之歸者益可驗
punctuated: 非天實右序我周乎？故使我薄言震動於諸侯也，大國之侯伯、小國之子男，莫不震懼於方嶽之下；懷柔百於百神也，深廣之河、崇高之嶽，莫不感格於祭告之時，則信乎武王之為天下君矣。君天下既驗於人神之帰，保天命尤在於政教之舉。故又言明昭乎我周也，既以慶讓黜陟之典，式序在位之諸侯：有功有徳者，則有加地進律之賞；不敬不順者，則有黜地削爵之罰。彼稱干比戈，昔以戡亂者，今則戢之而弗試；張弓挾矢，昔以伐罪者，今則櫜之而弗用。父子之親、君臣之義，懿徳也，我則益求之以布于中國，以敦教化；長幼之序、夫婦之別，懿徳也，我則益求之以陳于華夏，以厚風俗，則信乎武王之能保天命矣。吁！始焉天眷不敢必者，以見武王敬天之心也；終焉天命之保深可信者，以見武王克盡為君之道也。詩人其善於美盛徳之形容者歟！抑考之，《槩》亦巡守而作。其曰「堕山喬嶽，允猶翕河」，即懷柔百神事也；其曰「敷天之下，裒時之對」，即震疊諸侯事也。讀者合而觀之，則周家所以得神人之帰者益可驗。
translation_en:
…is it not that Heaven truly honors and establishes our Zhou in the succession? Thus, when it causes us to stir and awe the feudal lords, the marquises and earls of great states and the viscounts and barons of small states are all without exception awestruck beneath the directional sacred peaks; and when we soothe and appease all [?] the hundred spirits, the deep and wide Yellow River and the lofty sacred peaks are all without exception moved to respond at the time of the sacrificial announcements—truly, then, King Wu is the sovereign of all under Heaven!

While being sovereign of all under Heaven is already verified by the allegiance of men and spirits, preserving the Mandate of Heaven lies even more in the institution of governance and moral instruction. Therefore, the ode goes on to say: Brightly illustrious is our Zhou! Having used the statutes of reward, reprimand, demotion, and promotion to rank in due order the feudal lords in their positions, those who possess merit and virtue receive the reward of increased territory and advanced ritual rank, whereas those who are irreverent and disobedient suffer the punishment of reduced territory and stripped nobility. Those shields raised and halberds aligned, formerly used to quell rebellion, are now gathered in and not put to the test; those bows drawn and arrows clasped, formerly used to punish the guilty, are now encased and not put to use. The affection between father and son and the righteousness between ruler and minister are admirable virtues; we seek them out all the more to spread them throughout the Central States, so as to strengthen moral transformation. The order between elder and younger and the distinction between husband and wife are admirable virtues; we seek them out all the more to set them forth across Huaxia, so as to enrich customs. Truly, then, King Wu is able to preserve the Mandate of Heaven!

Ah! At the beginning, not daring to take Heaven's favor for granted reveals King Wu's heart of reverence toward Heaven; at the end, the deep credibility of his preserving the Mandate of Heaven reveals King Wu's ability to fulfill completely the Way of being a sovereign. How skilled was the poet in praising the manifestation of abundant virtue! Moreover, upon examination, the ode "Ban" [?] ("Pan" 般) was also composed for a tour of inspection. What it calls "the long-ridged mountains and lofty peaks, and the flooding Yellow River truly following its course" refers precisely to the matter of soothing and appeasing the hundred spirits; what it calls "under the whole expanse of Heaven, gathering those who respond to him" refers precisely to the matter of awing the feudal lords. If the reader views them together, how the House of Zhou won the allegiance of spirits and men can be verified all the more clearly.

translation_en:
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"The Marquis of Qi sent his younger brother Nian to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" [Seventh year of Duke Yin]; "The Earl of Zheng sent Yuan to come and surrender Beng" [Eighth year of Duke Yin]; "Men of Song and men of Wei entered Zheng" [Tenth year of Duke Yin]; "The Duke, together with the Marquis of Qi and the Earl of Zheng, entered Xu" [Eleventh year of Duke Yin]; "Men of Cai, men of Wei, and men of Chen followed the King to attack Zheng" [Fifth year of Duke Huan]; "Men of Qin entered Ruo" [Fifth year of Duke Wen]; "Men of Chu attacked Zheng" [Ninth year of Duke Wen]; "The Viscount of Chu sent Jiao to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" [Ninth year of Duke Wen]; "The Earl of Qin sent Shu to come on a mission of friendly inquiries" [Twelfth year of Duke Wen]; "The Duke met with the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Earl of Cao, and Zhao Dun of Jin; on the guiyou day, they joined in a covenant together at Xincheng" [Fourteenth year of Duke Wen].

Liu Xuan 劉宣

Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary (zhushi) Qian: Although this topic compares many entries, its purport is quite easy to see. Most writers failed to grasp it truly, setting forth vague arguments without arriving at a clear conclusion. Only this essay possesses decisive judgment as well as modulation of tone, and its conclusion is especially fine.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan) Li: In studying the Spring and Autumn Annals, what is valued is the ability to elucidate the Sage's intent. The divisions of this topic are very clear, and originally there is nothing difficult to understand about it; yet because the various missions of friendly inquiries and military campaigns are heterogeneous, writers had no way to weigh and reconcile them, thus entirely losing the fundamental purport. This essay does not lose it, and its prose elucidates the meaning well; it rightly belongs among those selected.

Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler (xiuzhuan) Lin: Righteous in principle and austere in diction, it captures the purport of the Sage's praise and blame, and is truly an excellent piece of work.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
考試官學士江批
〔以人心有周為王道幸以人心有晉為世道幸深得聖人作經之旨〕
侯度紊春秋幸諸侯之從王外勢張春秋幸諸侯之
從伯是可以驗人心禮義之天猶未泯也當我隱公
初年王靈不振啓列國之放恣者誰耶齊鄭宋魯衛
也齊不念夾輔之舊勳欲黨魯而遣弟來聘則典禮
隳矣鄭不思王室之懿親欲結魯而使宛歸祊則疆
場壞矣不越二載宋恣鄭之伐已連衛侯以入鄭鄭
欲許之歸已扳齊魯以入許則邦交之禮由是廢矣
===
侯度之紊如此尚何望人心之有周乎是時桓王怒
鄭不朝而躬行天討所幸者姬姓若蔡衛既悉索敝
賦以從而罔敢差池三恪如陳侯復奔問官守以隨
而罔敢違越相天威於行在之所嚴號令於不臣之
邦雖曰無功而還亦足以警侯度於既紊矣春秋得
不為王道幸乎迨我文公中葉晉伯驟衰啓中國之
外懼者誰耶秦伯楚子也秦懷貳楚之忿稱兵入鄀
而逞志乎商密之墟則戎強于西矣楚啓北方之圖
出師伐鄭而蹂躪乎狼淵之境則荆盛于南矣曾幾

有晉爲世道幸深得聖人作經之旨
侯度棻春秋幸諸侯之從王外勢張春秋幸諸侯之
從伯是可以驗人心禮義之天猶未泯也當我隱公

也齊不念夾輔之舊勳欲黨魯而遣弟來聘則典禮
隳矣鄭不思王室之懿親欲結魯而使宛歸祊則疆
埸壞矣不越二載宋怨鄭之伐已連衛侯以入鄭鄭
欲許之歸已拔齊魯以入許則邦交之禮由是廢矣
===
侯度之棻如此尚何望人心之有周乎是時桓王怒
鄭不朝而躬行天討所幸者姬姓若蔡衛既悉索敝
賦以從而罔敢差池三恪如陳侯復奔問官守以隨
而罔敢違越相天威於行在之所嚴號令於不臣之
邦雖曰無功而還亦是以警侯度於既棻矣春秋得
不爲王道幸乎迨我文公中葉晉伯驟衰啓中國之
外懼者誰耶秦伯楚子也秦懷貳楚之忿稱兵入鄀
而逕造乎商密之墟則戎强于西矣楚啓北方之圖
出師伐鄭而蹂躪乎狼淵之境則荆盛于南矣曾幾
punctuated:
考試官學士江批：〔以人心有周為王道幸，以人心有晉為世道幸，深得聖人作經之旨。〕

侯度紊，春秋幸諸侯之從王；外勢張，春秋幸諸侯之從伯。是可以驗人心禮義之天猶未泯也。當我隱公初年，王靈不振，啓列國之放恣者誰耶？齊、鄭、宋、魯、衛也。齊不念夾輔之舊勳，欲黨魯而遣弟來聘，則典禮隳矣；鄭不思王室之懿親，欲結魯而使宛歸祊，則疆場壞矣。不越二載，宋恣鄭之伐已，連衛侯以入鄭；鄭欲許之歸已，扳齊、魯以入許，則邦交之禮由是廢矣。侯度之紊如此，尚何望人心之有周乎？是時桓王怒鄭不朝，而躬行天討。所幸者，姬姓若蔡、衛，既悉索敝賦以從，而罔敢差池；三恪如陳侯，復奔問官守以隨，而罔敢違越。相天威於行在之所，嚴號令於不臣之邦。雖曰無功而還，亦足以警侯度於既紊矣。春秋得不為王道幸乎？迨我文公中葉，晉伯驟衰，啓中國之外懼者誰耶？秦伯、楚子也。秦懷貳楚之忿，稱兵入鄀，而逞志乎商密之墟，則戎強于西矣；楚啓北方之圖，出師伐鄭，而蹂躪乎狼淵之境，則荆盛于南矣。曾幾
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner and Chancellor Jiang: 〔Taking the people's hearts remaining with Zhou as fortunate for the Kingly Way, and taking the people's hearts remaining with Jin as fortunate for the way of the world, this deeply grasps the Sage's intent in composing the Classic.〕

When the proper bounds of the feudal lords were thrown into disorder, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) considered it fortunate that the feudal lords followed the King; when external powers expanded, the Spring and Autumn Annals considered it fortunate that the feudal lords followed the Hegemon. Through this, one can verify that the heavenly nature of ritual and righteousness in people's hearts had not yet been extinguished.

In the early years of our Duke Yin, the royal prestige was unroused; who was it that initiated the unbridled license of the various states? It was Qi, Zheng, Song, Lu, and Wei. Qi did not remember its old merits of assisting the royal house, and wishing to form a faction with Lu, sent its ruler's younger brother to come on a mission of friendly inquiry—thus the canonical rites were ruined. Zheng did not reflect upon its close kinship with the royal house, and wishing to form a bond with Lu, sent Yuan to turn over Beng—thus the territorial boundaries were corrupted. Within no more than two years, Song, resenting [?] Zheng's attacks on itself, joined with the Marquis of Wei to invade Zheng; Zheng, wishing to make Xu submit to itself, drew in Qi and Lu to invade Xu—and from this the rites of interstate relations were abandoned. With the proper bounds of the feudal lords thrown into such disorder, how could one still hope that people's hearts held any regard for Zhou? At this time, King Huan grew angry that Zheng did not come to court, and personally executed Heaven's punitive expedition. What was fortunate was that states of the Ji clan such as Cai and Wei exhausted their humble levies to follow him without daring to falter; and among the Three Revered States (sanke), the Marquis of Chen likewise hurried to inquire after the King's officials and guards, accompanying him without daring to transgress. They assisted the heavenly majesty at the temporary royal headquarters and enforced strict commands upon an unsubmissive state. Although it is said they returned without success, it was still sufficient to admonish the feudal lords after their proper bounds had already fallen into disorder. How could the Spring and Autumn Annals not consider this fortunate for the Kingly Way?

Coming to the middle years of our Duke Wen, the hegemony of Jin suddenly declined; who was it that initiated the external fears of the Central States? It was the Earl of Qin and the Viscount of Chu. Qin, harboring anger over Ruo's [?] double-dealing toward Chu, raised troops to invade Ruo and worked its will upon the ruins of Shangmi—thus the Rong grew strong in the west. Chu, opening its designs upon the north, sent forth an army to attack Zheng and trampled the borders of Langyuan—thus Jing grew flourishing in the south. Scarcely how much…

translation_en:
…little time had passed before the people of Chu sent Yue Jiao under the pretext of presenting jade and silk to spy on Lu, and Qin ordered Qi Shu under the guise of ritual courtesy to pry into Lu; thus their ambitions to usurp the hegemony could no longer be concealed. With external powers expanding like this, how could one still hope that people's hearts would remain with Jin? At this time, Duke Ling of Jin sought to unite the feudal lords, and there was the covenant at Xincheng. Fortunately, states commanding respect like Song and Lu joined with the Marquis of Wei to come together, while previously wavering states like Chen and Zheng led Cao and Xu to arrive alongside them. They deliberated on policies to keep Chu out and planned strategies regarding Zhu. Although it is said that Zhao Dun presided over the covenant, it was still sufficient to check [?] external powers just as they were expanding. Could the Sage not rejoice on behalf of the moral order of the world? Ah! In the beginning, because the three states followed the King, he rejoiced that the righteous duty between ruler and minister was made clear; in the end, because the seven states followed the Hegemon, he rejoiced that the distinction between barbarian and Chinese was rectified. How profound was the Sage's noble intention to uphold the moral order of the world! Even so, had King Huan been able to redirect the army that attacked Zheng to call Song and Lu to account for the manner in which their rulers gained their states, then the law of the Nine Punitive Expeditions would have been carried out, and the governance of Kings Wen and Wu could have been restored; had Duke Ling been able to turn the covenant at Xincheng into an undertaking like those at Shaoling and Chengpu, then the righteousness of uniting and rectifying the realm would have been manifest, and the achievements of Dukes Huan and Wen could have been equaled [?]. Alas, what a pity that they possessed the opportunity to act yet did not do so, merely arousing the sighs of later generations! Alas!

其欲得諸侯以成創伯之功人莫不以為易矣抑孰

translation_en:
…meetings and covenants yet lost the feudal lords, his reputation was weaker than that of Duke Wen of Jin, though his reality was flourishing; through Duke Wen of Jin's three meetings and covenants in which he won over the feudal lords, his reputation was more flourishing than that of Duke Huan of Qi, though his reality was in decline. When we compare the events and examine them, the relative superiority and inferiority of the two hegemons become apparent.

Moreover, in the Spring and Autumn period, when speaking of founding the hegemony one refers to Duke Huan of Qi, and when speaking of continuing the hegemony one refers to Duke Wen of Jin. With respect to the reputation and reality of the two dukes, how indeed can one see their relative superiority and inferiority?

Now, Duke Huan of Qi, possessing a great state east of the mountains and following upon the minor hegemony of Duke Xi of Qi, from the time he pacified Song at Beixing onward, wished to win over the feudal lords so as to accomplish the merit of founding the hegemony—and there was no one who did not consider it easy. Yet who would have known that in a time when the various states lacked a unifying authority, and the Kingly Way had just transformed into hegemony, people's minds could not avoid harboring doubts? Therefore, when he assembled them twice at Juan, Song and Chen submitted, yet Lu did not come; when he covenanted twice at You, Lu and Zheng followed, yet Wei did not arrive; and it even came to the point that the two rulers of Chen and Cai both failed to participate in the campaigns at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu. Thus, if one compares Huan with Wen, given Huan's difficulty in winning the multitude, his reputation seemed weaker than Wen's. However, if we investigate the reality and discuss it, Duke Huan fostered trustworthiness and righteousness at the meetings of Juan and the covenants of You, so that his hegemonic enterprise daily approached completion; and he exhausted his efforts in supporting and upholding the royal house at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu, so that his hegemonic enterprise daily grew more flourishing. How could that be compared to Duke Wen, who suddenly flourished and immediately declined? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) praised the flourishing of his reality without dwelling on his reputation. How great, then, was Huan's superiority over Wen!

Duke Wen of Jin, as a scion of the hereditary line blessed with "granaries of millet and bows of horn" [Juhe, the royal gift to Marquis Wen of Jin], and after having personally experienced perils and hardships, from the time he entered the state from Quwo onward, wished to win over the feudal lords so as to plan the enterprise of continuing the hegemony—and there was no one who did not consider it difficult. Yet who would have known that in a day when the feudal lords were in turmoil, once the line of hegemony was again continued in the Central States, there was no one whose heart did not find a place to turn in allegiance? 國聽命，而非若于幽之失衛；以至上而王臣之王子虎，下而列國之大夫，亦皆與於翟泉之歃，又非若首止、葵丘之失陳、失蔡焉。故以文較桓，則文得衆之易，其名若盛於桓矣。然究其實而論之，則文公假禮要君，雖驟致其盛，而犯名瀆分，遂即見其衰，求如桓公寖成而極盛，得乎？《春秋》所以全其名之盛而不掩其實也，文之劣於桓也又何如！所謂即諸侯從違之殊，見伯主名實之異，以此。雖然，桓之優於文也，非惟得諸侯之名實為然，其見諸事功亦然。桓公二十餘年蓄威養晦，始得問罪於楚；文公一駕，而城濮之功多於召陵。桓公屢盟屢會，邅回晚嵗，始會宰周公；文公再合諸侯，而温之事敏乎葵丘。是又見文公之功多於桓公者，罪亦多於桓公也；事速就乎桓公者，義尤壞乎桓公也。所以名盛乎桓公，而實亦衰乎桓公矣。是何也？良由二公存心之有正譎耳。噫！聖人之言，吾於是有足徵焉。

translation_en:
…states obeyed his commands, unlike losing Wei at the covenant of You; and finally, from the royal minister Wangzi Hu above to the grandees of the various states below, all participated in the blood-smearing covenant at Diquan, which again was unlike losing Chen and Cai at Shouzhi and Kuiqiu. Therefore, if we compare Duke Wen with Duke Huan, Duke Wen won over the multitude easily, and in reputation he seemed more flourishing than Duke Huan. Yet if we investigate the reality and discuss it, Duke Wen borrowed the guise of ritual to coerce his sovereign; although he suddenly achieved his height of power, by offending against nominal status and violating his proper station he immediately manifested his decline. Could he possibly hope to match Duke Huan’s gradual attainment of supreme flourishing? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) preserves the fullness of his reputation without concealing the reality—how clear, once again, is Duke Wen’s inferiority to Duke Huan! What is meant by discerning the difference between the reputation and reality of the hegemonic rulers from the differing compliance and defiance of the feudal lords is precisely this.

Even so, Duke Huan’s superiority to Duke Wen is true not only in the reputation and reality of winning over the feudal lords, but also as seen in their actual deeds and achievements. Duke Huan accumulated authority and nurtured his strength in obscurity for over twenty years before he was finally able to call Chu to account for its crimes; Duke Wen sortied just once, and his achievement at Chengpu exceeded that at Shaoling. Duke Huan held repeated covenants and assemblies, pacing back and forth until his late years before he finally met with the Grand宰 Duke of Zhou; Duke Wen assembled the feudal lords only twice, and the affair at Wen was accomplished more swiftly than that at Kuiqiu. From this we again see that where Duke Wen’s achievements exceeded those of Duke Huan, his offenses also exceeded those of Duke Huan; where his enterprises were accomplished more rapidly than Duke Huan’s, righteousness was ruined even more than under Duke Huan. Thus, while his reputation was grander than Duke Huan’s, in reality he declined more than Duke Huan. Why is this? It is truly because the intentions harbored by the two dukes differed in being upright versus crafty. Alas! In this I find sufficient verification for the words of the Sage.

君子之聽訟，既當辨其事情之實，尤當盡夫體察之公。夫聽訟將以用刑，宜君子所當慎也。苟於此不辨夫事情之實，而盡夫體察之公，又何以即天倫而不枉其人哉？記者之意若曰：五刑之訟，不可以槩議也。人之所犯雖同，而事情或異。且以事而言，則輕重各有其序，而不可亂焉，行其事者，其可無意論乎？謂之意論，以意生乎有惑故也。以情而言，則淺深各有其量，而不可過焉，原其情者，其可不慎測乎？謂之慎測，以慎由乎用誠故也。如是，則事情之輕重淺深，無不得其辨矣。不寧惟是，又必悉其聰，則所聽者審而無…

Comment by Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Shao 邵: On this topic, most candidates do not understand the explanation of what is light or grave and what is shallow or deep, and when it comes to sharpness of hearing and insight and loyalty and compassion, they treat them only superficially. This essay alone hits the mark in both expression and principle; none who is not thoroughly versed in this Classic could have written it. It is without doubt a top selection.

Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Lin 林: In framing its central thesis around distinguishing the facts and circumstances and fully exercising empathetic observation, it has grasped the meaning.

Comment by Examiner and Academician Jiang 江: It elucidates the meaning of the superior man's care in hearing litigation and applying punishments thoroughly and without omission; an excellent piece.

In hearing litigation, the superior man must not only distinguish the reality of the facts and circumstances, but even more so fulfill the impartiality of empathetic observation. Now, hearing litigation is a prelude to applying punishments, and it is rightly something in which the superior man must exercise caution. If in doing so he does not distinguish the reality of the facts and circumstances and fulfill the impartiality of empathetic observation, how then could he accord with the natural human relationships and avoid wronging the people involved?

The meaning of the recorder of the text is as if to say: Litigation involving the Five Punishments cannot be judged by a single sweeping rule. Though the offenses men commit may be the same, the facts and circumstances may differ. Spoken of in terms of the facts of the deed, lightness and gravity each have their proper order and must not be confused; how could one who handles the case fail to weigh them with thoughtful judgment? It is called weighing with thoughtful judgment because such thought arises from the presence of doubt. Spoken of in terms of the motivating circumstances, shallowness and depth each have their measure and must not be exceeded; how could one who traces those circumstances fail to fathom them with care? It is called fathoming with care because such care comes from the exercise of sincerity. When this is done, there is nothing in the lightness or gravity, shallowness or depth of the facts and circumstances that is not properly distinguished.

Not only this: one must also apply to the full one's sharpness of hearing, so that what is heard is scrutinized and nothing…

text:

不欺之至也致其愛則不忍之至也明視聰聽而察
之於詞色之間忠愛惻怛而體之於言意之表如是
則人之是非曲直莫不得其情矣吁事情之辨既如

translation_en:
…nothing is missed; when he exhausts his keenness of sight, what he sees is precise and nothing is overlooked. When he extends his loyalty to the utmost, it is the pinnacle of non-deception; when he extends his affection to the utmost, it is the pinnacle of commiseration. Seeing clearly and hearing acutely, he examines them amidst their words and facial expressions; with loyal affection and sympathetic grief, he empathetically understands them beyond their spoken words and intentions. In this way, there is no case in which the right and wrong, the crooked and straight of people fail to have their true circumstances ascertained. Ah! Since the differentiation of the circumstances of the affair is already like that, and the impartiality of empathetic examination is furthermore like this, what more could be added to the Way of hearing litigation? Moreover, if we examine the preceding text, which says, "In all cases of hearing litigation involving the Five Punishments, one must trace the affection between father and son and establish the duty between ruler and minister in order to weigh them," this shows that when a father conceals for his son and a son conceals for his father, uprightness lies therein, because they possess the affection between father and son; whereas punishing a disorderly state with heavy penalties is done because it lacks the duty between ruler and minister. The following text also says, "In doubtful criminal cases, broadly share the deliberation with the multitude; if the multitude is in doubt, pardon them; one must examine precedents great and small in order to bring the judgment to completion." How thorough it is to such a degree! This, too, is what those who hear litigation and apply punishments ought to know.

"These six are the sounds of virtuous music. Only then does one harmonize them with bells, chime-stones, thirty-six-pipe mouth organs, and twenty-five-string zithers, and perform dances to them with shields, battle-axes, yak-tail pennants, and pheasant feathers."

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
作樂者
考試官學士江批請論先王作樂之道深得本旨
一薦何忝
既作夫質素之音復備夫聲容之盛此聖人作樂之
道也盖作樂之道貴乎衆樂之兼全也苟徒作夫質
素之音而不備夫聲容之盛又何以盡作樂之道哉
記樂君子謂夫古先聖王之作樂發諸聲音者寓之
象稽諸度數者寓之器故作六者之樂也此六者何
鞉鼓柷敔壎篪是已作革以為鞉鼓播之則中聲以
===
發焉作木以為柷敔擊之則中聲以節焉作土為壎
作竹為篪吹之則中聲以和焉凡此六者皆中聲之
所出質而不華素而不靡非要妙之音也豈不謂德
音之音乎聖人不惟以質素為本抑又越之金石以
為鐘磬則洋洋其盈耳宣之匏絲以為竽瑟則纍纍
如貫珠是皆華美之音也而必曰和之者所以諧其
聲也武執干戚則干為朱楯而戚為玉斧也文執旄
狄則旄為牛尾而狄為雉羽也是皆樂舞之器也而
必曰舞之者所以動其容也豈不謂聲容之盛乎先

既作夫質素之音，復備夫聲容之盛，此聖人作樂之道也。盖作樂之道，貴乎衆樂之兼全也。苟徒作夫質素之音，而不備夫聲容之盛，又何以盡作樂之道哉？記樂君子謂：夫古先聖王之作樂，發諸聲音者寓之象，稽諸度數者寓之器，故作六者之樂也。此六者何？鞉鼓、柷敔、壎篪是已。作革以為鞉鼓，播之則中聲以發焉；作木以為柷敔，擊之則中聲以節焉；作土為壎，作竹為篪，吹之則中聲以和焉。凡此六者，皆中聲之所出，質而不華，素而不靡，非要妙之音也，豈不謂德音之音乎？聖人不惟以質素為本，抑又越之金石以為鐘磬，則洋洋其盈耳；宣之匏絲以為竽瑟，則纍纍如貫珠。是皆華美之音也，而必曰「和之」者，所以諧其聲也。武執干戚，則干為朱楯而戚為玉斧也；文執旄狄，則旄為牛尾而狄為雉羽也。是皆樂舞之器也，而必曰「舞之」者，所以動其容也。豈不謂聲容之盛乎？先
