…those who make music.

Examiner and Chancellor Jiang comments: This discussion [請 -> 諸/講?] of the Way in which the former kings created music deeply grasps the fundamental purport; how could there be any shame in recommending it?

Having created the sounds of plainness and simplicity, they further provided the fullness of acoustic and visual display—this is the Way in which the sages created music. For the Way of creating music values the comprehensive completeness of all the instruments of music. If one merely creates the sounds of plainness and simplicity without providing the fullness of acoustic and visual display, how then could one exhaust the Way of creating music? The gentleman who recorded the Record of Music meant to say: In the creation of music by the ancient sage-kings, that which issued forth in sound and tone was lodged in symbolic forms, and that which was examined according to pitch-standards and numerical measures was lodged in instruments; therefore they made the music of the "six things." What are these six? They are the pellet-drum and large drum (taogu), the starter-box and stopper-tiger (zhuyu), and the ocarina and transverse flute (xunchi). They worked leather to make the pellet-drum and large drum; when shaken and beaten, the centered tones are thereby initiated. They worked wood to make the starter-box and stopper-tiger; when struck, the centered tones are thereby regulated. They worked clay to make the ocarina and worked bamboo to make the transverse flute; when blown, the centered tones are thereby harmonized. All six of these are that from which the centered tones emerge—substantial and unornamented, plain and unextravagant, not subtle or alluring sounds. Must they not be called the tones of virtuous sound? The sages not only took plainness and simplicity as the foundation, but also rang them forth in metal and stone to make bells and musical stones (zhongqing), so that vast and flowing they fill the ears; and spread them out through gourd and silk to make mouth-organs and zithers (yuse), so that in continuous succession they are like strung pearls. These are all ornate and beautiful sounds, and the reason the text necessarily says "to harmonize them" is that by this means their tones are brought into accord. In the martial dance they hold shields and battle-axes (ganqi), where the gan is a vermilion shield and the qi is a jade-decorated axe; in the civil dance they hold yak-tail pennants and pheasant plumes (maodi), where the mao is an ox-tail and the di is a pheasant feather. These are all implements of musical dance, and the reason the text necessarily says "to dance them" is that by this means their physical movements are set in motion. 其幽足以交於神而明足以交於人行之當時莫不

… Kings created music in this manner, then the eight timbres could be brought into harmony without encroaching upon one another's proper order—how could there be even a single instance of disharmony? In general, how could the Former Kings' creation of music have been done in vain? Thus, its function is great indeed. In the unseen realm, it suffices to commune with the spirits, and in the visible realm, it suffices to bring people into fellowship; practiced in its own time, nothing fails to attain what is fitting, and displayed to later generations, nothing fails to attain its proper order. title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
下也而是以正人心於萬世此善論孟子者不以得行
道為功而以正人心為功則功不在禹下也可見矣
請申論之處賓師之位而有泰山巖巖之氣象者孟
子也承堯舜之統而無罅隙之可議者大禹也大禹
有功於前孟子有功於後而孟子功不在禹下之言
宜無待於辨矣彼乃有人曰禹達而在上孟子窮而
在下孟子之功誠在於禹下矣是何不下於禹哉此
蓋以位之窮達論孟子非真知孟子者也彼復有人
曰禹居上世而天下乃治孟子當戰國而爭雄不已
===

達言而治亂論耶特以其時之不偶也時之不偶亦
孟子之不偶也孟子之不偶實當時之偶也使孟子
生於戰國之前則楊墨孰與距乎楊墨弗距則天下
不復知有仁義矣使孟子生於戰國之後則人心孰
與正乎人心弗正則天下不復知有正道矣此天生

說是以爲萬古不易之定論養氣之說是以擴前聖
punctuated: 下也，而是以正人心於萬世。此善論孟子者，不以得行道為功，而以正人心為功，則功不在禹下也可見矣。請申論之。處賓師之位，而有泰山巖巖之氣象者，孟子也；承堯舜之統，而無罅隙之可議者，大禹也。大禹有功於前，孟子有功於後，而「孟子功不在禹下」之言，宜無待於辨矣。彼乃有人曰：「禹達而在上，孟子窮而在下，孟子之功誠在於禹下矣，是何不下於禹哉？」此蓋以位之窮達論孟子，非真知孟子者也。彼復有人曰：「禹居上世而天下乃治，孟子當戰國而爭雄不已，孟子之功實居於禹下矣，曽何不下於禹哉？」此蓋以世之治亂論孟子，非善論孟子者也。孟子豈可以窮達言而治亂論耶？特以其時之不偶也。時之不偶，亦孟子之不偶也；孟子之不偶，實當時之偶也。使孟子生於戰國之前，則楊墨孰與距乎？楊墨弗距，則天下不復知有仁義矣。使孟子生於戰國之後，則人心孰與正乎？人心弗正，則天下不復知有正道矣。此天生孟子於戰國之時，亦將有功於當時也。是以性善之說，足以爲萬古不易之定論；養氣之說，足以擴前聖
translation_en: … inferior to Yu's, yet by this means he rectified human hearts for ten thousand generations. Thus, one who is skilled at evaluating Mencius does not reckon his achievement by whether he succeeded in putting the Way into practice, but rather by his rectifying of human hearts; from this it can be seen that his achievement was not inferior to Yu's. Let me elaborate upon this. Occupying the position of guest and teacher, while possessing a bearing as lofty and craggy as Mount Tai—such was Mencius; succeeding to the line of Yao and Shun, without a single flaw that could be criticized—such was the Great Yu. The Great Yu had achievements in former times, and Mencius had achievements in later times; thus the saying that "Mencius's achievement is not inferior to Yu's" should require no debate. Yet there are some who say: "Yu was prominent and occupied a high position, whereas Mencius was inadversity and remained below; Mencius's achievement is truly inferior to Yu's—how could it not be inferior to Yu's?" This is to evaluate Mencius on the basis of adversity or prominence of position; such people do not truly know Mencius. And there are others who say: "Yu lived in high antiquity and the world was thereby brought to order, whereas Mencius lived during the Warring States period when contention for supremacy never ceased; Mencius's achievement truly ranks below Yu's—how could it not be inferior to Yu's?" This is to evaluate Mencius on the basis of the order or disorder of the age; such people are not skilled at evaluating Mencius. How could Mencius be spoken of in terms of adversity and prominence, or evaluated in terms of order and disorder? It was simply that his times were unpropitious. That the times were unpropitious was also Mencius's misfortune; yet Mencius's misfortune was in truth the good fortune of that age. Had Mencius been born before the Warring States period, who then would have resisted Yang Zhu and Mo Di? Had Yang and Mo not been resisted, the world would no longer have known that benevolence and righteousness exist. Had Mencius been born after the Warring States period, who then would have rectified human hearts? Had human hearts not been rectified, the world would no longer have known that the correct Way exists. Therefore, Heaven's giving birth to Mencius in the time of the Warring States was also so that he would perform a great service for that age. Accordingly, his doctrine of the goodness of human nature suffices to serve as an immutable, definitive judgment for ten thousand ages; his doctrine of nourishing the vital氣 (qi) suffices to expand upon what the former sages…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
未發之蘊奥正異端息邪說若誅夷之斧鉞距詖行
放淫辭若中流之砥柱故地平天成萬世永頼人皆
知禹之功大也而不知天理既晦而復明者伊誰之
功歟隨山濬川疏通九河人皆知禹之功大也而不
知民彝既墜而復振者伊誰之力歟况禹之平水土
惟恐陷溺其人之身孟子之闢邪說惟恐陷溺其人
之心溺其身者身雖死而天理猶在溺其心者身雖
存而天理已滅是知拯人之身者其功固不小正人
之心者其功亦甚大由是論之則孟子功不在禹下
===
之論瞭然矣雖然論孟子非小其禹之功也言禹非
大其孟子之功也舉大禹則孟子之功以明言孟子
則大禹之功益顯大哉孟子之功乎誠所以正人心
而不下於大禹者乎竊嘗疑之孟子者得孔子所傳
之道而孔子亦窮而在下者也孟子之功既不在禹
下孔子何無功焉意有是哉觀之宰予曰以予觀於
夫子賢於堯舜遠矣是堯舜之道非孔子無以明則
知孔子之功非特不在堯舜之下而反有過於堯舜
矣以是推之先儒孟子功不在禹下之言豈欺我哉

punctuated: 未發之蘊奥；正異端、息邪說，若誅夷之斧鉞；距詖行、放淫辭，若中流之砥柱。故地平天成，萬世永頼，人皆知禹之功大也，而不知天理既晦而復明者，伊誰之功歟？隨山濬川，疏通九河，人皆知禹之功大也，而不知民彝既墜而復振者，伊誰之力歟？况禹之平水土，惟恐陷溺其人之身；孟子之闢邪說，惟恐陷溺其人之心。溺其身者，身雖死而天理猶在；溺其心者，身雖存而天理已滅。是知拯人之身者，其功固不小；正人之心者，其功亦甚大。由是論之，則「孟子功不在禹下」之論瞭然矣。雖然，論孟子非小其禹之功也，言禹非大其孟子之功也。舉大禹則孟子之功以明，言孟子則大禹之功益顯。大哉孟子之功乎！誠所以正人心而不下於大禹者乎！竊嘗疑之：孟子者，得孔子所傳之道，而孔子亦窮而在下者也；孟子之功既不在禹下，孔子何無功焉？意有是哉！觀之宰予曰：「以予觀於夫子，賢於堯、舜遠矣。」是堯、舜之道非孔子無以明，則知孔子之功非特不在堯、舜之下，而反有過於堯、舜矣。以是推之，先儒「孟子功不在禹下」之言，豈欺我哉！
translation_en: … the profound mysteries unrevealed by [former sages]; his rectifying of heterodoxies and putting to rest of perverse doctrines were like the battle-axes of execution and extermination; his resisting of one-sided actions and banishing of licentious expressions were like a pillar standing firm in midstream. Thus, when the earth was leveled and heaven’s order completed, so that ten thousand generations could forever rely upon it, everyone knows that the achievement of Yu 禹 was great—yet whose achievement was it that the Principle of Heaven, once obscured, was made bright again? In following the mountains, dredging the rivers, and channeling the Nine Rivers, everyone knows that the achievement of Yu was great—yet by whose strength was it that the moral norms of the people, once fallen into ruin, were revived? Moreover, when Yu brought peace to the waters and the land, his only fear was that people’s physical bodies would be drowned; when Mencius 孟子 refuted perverse doctrines, his only fear was that people’s minds would be drowned. When one’s body is drowned, though the body dies, the Principle of Heaven still remains; when one’s mind is drowned, though the body survives, the Principle of Heaven is already extinguished. From this we know that the achievement of saving people’s bodies is certainly not small, and the achievement of rectifying people’s minds is also exceedingly great. Discussed from this perspective, the proposition that "the achievement of Mencius is not inferior to that of Yu" becomes crystal clear. Even so, discussing Mencius does not belittle the achievement of Yu, and speaking of Yu does not exaggerate the achievement of Mencius. By citing Great Yu, the achievement of Mencius is made clear; by speaking of Mencius, the achievement of Great Yu becomes all the more manifest. Great indeed is the achievement of Mencius! Truly, is it not because he rectified people’s minds that he is not inferior to Great Yu? I have privately wondered about this: Mencius obtained the Way transmitted by Confucius 孔子, and Confucius too was one who lived in困窮 (distress) and in a lowly station; since the achievement of Mencius is not inferior to that of Yu, how could Confucius be without achievement? Could there really be such a thing! Look at what Zai Yu 宰予 said: "As I view the Master, he is far worthier than Yao 堯 and Shun 舜." Since the Way of Yao and Shun could not have been made clear without Confucius, we know that the achievement of Confucius is not merely not inferior to that of Yao and Shun, but in fact surpasses Yao and Shun. Inferring from this, how could the words of the former Confucian that "the achievement of Mencius is not inferior to that of Yu" deceive us!

Memorial

A Simulated Memorial by the Inheritor of the Enfeoffment as Duke for Fulfilling the Sage (Yansheng gong 衍聖公) Giving Thanks for the Imperial Carriage Performing the Libation and Offering Ceremony (shidian 釋奠) to the Former Teacher (Confucius)

Wu Fu 吳福
Associate Examiner, Bureau Secretary Qian 錢, comments: "The memorial is fine."
Associate Examiner, Senior Compiler Li 李, comments: "The memorial is fitting in style."
Examiner, Senior Compiler Lin 林, comments: "Classic and elegant."
Examiner, Academician Jiang 江, comments: "The memorial is smooth and well-balanced."

Your servant So-and-so humbly considers that as all within the seas and the realm enjoys cultural brilliance, the Way of the Six Classics is greatly elucidated; and that in performing the libation and offering ceremony in the temple court, the August Person of Ten Thousand Chariots has personally exerted himself. The community of scholars increases in joy, and the distant descendants [of Confucius] are richly blessed. This is all because we humbly encounter Your Majesty the Emperor, who is perspicacious, intelligent, far-seeing, and wise, divinely sage, martial, and civil. Your virtue matches that of the Three Kings, truly embodying King Wen's gazing toward the Way; your achievements rival those of the line of former imperial sages, ever more honoring the Former Sage in order to exalt culture. The imperial carriage halted its progress at the ringed-water gates of the imperial academy (qiaomen 橋門), and jade and silk were presented with libations in the hall of rites. The bamboo and wooden ritual vessels were given added adornment, and the jade libation ladles were wielded with solemn deportment. Listening to the sound of bells and drums and the notes of flutes and pipes, people submit to and practice the rites and music of the Sacred Dynasty; gazing up at the beauty of the ancestral temple and the rich array of the hundred officials, the walls and gates of the Master's school are raised ever higher. Your modest radiance shines forth beyond all former accounts, and your luminous virtue wafts its fragrance to future generations. Since the Three Dynasties…

translation_en:
… the Three Dynasties onward, there has never been anything more flourishing than today. Your servant So-and-so is by nature ordinary and mediocre, yet unworthily continues the lineage of the Former Teacher; my learning is of no benefit, yet I have undeservedly received investiture with an illustrious title. In emulating the worthy, I am deeply ashamed before my predecessors; in witnessing the exaltation of virtue, I rejoice at encountering this flourishing age. My praise cannot be exhausted, and my gratitude is profound indeed. I humbly pray that with schools in the capital, academies in the districts, and halls in the subdistricts, the Sagely Way may be made ever more prosperous without end; and that with carriages sharing the same axle-width, writing sharing the same characters, and conduct sharing the same moral principles, the Imperial rule may be eternally consolidated for all time. Your servant is overcome with the utmost emotion and trepidation as I gaze up at Heaven and look up to the Sage, and I reverently present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's hearing.

對：倫理之在於人者，萬古同一心；倫理之著於書者，萬聖同一旨。蓋前聖所以垂世立教者，此倫理也；後聖所以敷言闡教者，亦此倫理也。倫理洽於人心，政教達於天下，先聖後聖，其揆一也。粤稽諸古：堯之「克明俊德，以親九族」，舜之「重華協帝」、「慎徽五典」，成湯之「肇修人紀」，武王之「重民五教」，此二帝三王皆重於倫理者也。洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝以至聖之德，君主億兆，慮民俗之未淳，故動三編之《誥》，如「五教育民」、「申明五常」，而告誡諄切，是皆篤厚於倫理也。迨至太宗文皇帝纘承丕緒，益恢前烈，欲民行善與孝，故著《為善陰隲》、《孝順事實》二書。宣宗章皇帝繼體守成，勵精圖治，欲民盡綱常之道，故著為《五倫書》，亦皆以倫理為重也。雖然，古今
translation_en:
Examiner Senior Compiler Lin 林 comments: "The answers given are detailed and clear; judging everything by the shared mind of the sages regarding human ethical relationships, it has hit the mark."
Examiner Academician Jiang 江 comments: "Its exposition and analysis of the purport of valuing human ethical relationships may be called thorough and worthy of selection."

Reply: As for human ethical relationships (lunli) residing in mankind, ten thousand ages share a single mind; as for human ethical relationships set forth in books, ten thousand sages share a single purport. Indeed, that by which the former sages handed down teachings for the world is these ethical relationships; that by which the later sages set forth words to elucidate teachings is likewise these ethical relationships. When ethical relationships permeate human hearts and governance and instruction reach throughout the realm, the former sages and later sages follow a single principle. Examining antiquity: Yao's "being able to make illustrious his lofty virtue, so as to endear the nine branches of the kin," Shun's "double radiance in harmony with the Emperor" and "carefully beautifying the five cardinal duties," Cheng Tang's "initiating the cultivation of human bonds," and King Wu's "attaching importance for the people to the five teachings"—these Two Emperors and Three Kings all placed great weight upon ethical relationships. Humbly reflecting upon our dynasty: Emperor Gao, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu 高皇帝), with the virtue of the utmost sage, ruled as sovereign over the hundreds of millions. Concerned that the customs of the people were not yet pure and simple, he therefore set forth the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Gao 大誥), with sections such as "Instructing the People in the Five Teachings" and "Reiterating the Five Constant Virtues," admonishing them earnestly and切ly—all of this showed deep devotion to ethical relationships. Coming down to Emperor Wen, the Grand Ancestor (Taizong 文皇帝), he succeeded to the great patrimony and further expanded the achievements of his predecessor. Wishing the people to practice goodness and filial piety, he therefore composed the two books Hidden Retribution for Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi 為善陰隲) and True Records of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi 孝順事實). Emperor Zhang, the Proclaiming Ancestor (Xuanzong 章皇帝), succeeded to the body of the state and conserved what had been accomplished, rousing his spirit to seek good governance. Wishing the people to fulfill the Way of the Three Bonds and Five Constant Virtues, he therefore composed the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu 五倫書)—all likewise placing great weight upon ethical relationships. Even so, ancient and modern…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
雖異世而同此道先後雖異時而同此心
三聖之心同一重倫理其與堯舜湯武之心為無間
三聖之書同一明倫理其與堯舜湯武之言為不殊
誥之所謂君臣同遊即書元首明哉股肱良哉
之旨也事實所謂降衷秉彝即書若有恒性之
意也陰隲言為善獲報是即書言惠迪吉從逆
凶也五倫言以綱常為治亦即書言彝倫攸叙
也與之同符合轍者在是宜乎同傳乎千萬世
之久而無窮也若夫宏綱大旨如為民造福勸
===
人行孝勉人為善教以人倫其要不外於是焉
然而孝為百行冠冕萬善本根雖云孝為一事
而五倫之理無不貫孰謂孝止於一事而已耶
傳曰事親孝故忠可移於君斯言也愚於終篇
獻不識可乎
第二問
陳嘉猷
同考試官訓導邵批所答詳明有斷制讀之令
人竦然可嘉

人竦然可嘉
punctuated:
雖異世而同此道，先後雖異時而同此心。三聖之心同一重倫理，其與堯、舜、湯、武之心為無間；三聖之書同一明倫理，其與堯、舜、湯、武之言為不殊。《誥》之所謂「君臣同遊」，即《書》「元首明哉，股肱良哉」之旨也；《事實》所謂「降衷秉彝」，即《書》「若有恒性」之意也；《陰隲》言為善獲報，是即《書》言「惠迪吉，從逆凶」也；《五倫》言以綱常為治，亦即《書》言「彝倫攸叙」也。與之同符合轍者在是，宜乎同傳乎千萬世之久而無窮也。若夫宏綱大旨，如為民造福、勸人行孝、勉人為善、教以人倫，其要不外於是焉。然而孝為百行冠冕、萬善本根，雖云孝為一事，而五倫之理無不貫，孰謂孝止於一事而已耶？《傳》曰：「事親孝，故忠可移於君。」斯言也，愚於終篇獻，不識可乎？

第二問
陳嘉猷
同考試官訓導邵批：所答詳明有斷制，讀之令人竦然，可嘉。
translation_en:
… though belonging to different ages, share this same Way; and preceding and succeeding times, though different eras, share this same mind. The minds of our Three Sacred Emperors are one in prizing human moral relationships, with no gap between them and the minds of Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wu; the books of our Three Sacred Emperors are one in illuminating human moral relationships, no different from the words of Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wu. What the Grand Pronouncements (Gao) call "ruler and minister roaming in harmony" is the purport of the Book of Documents (Shu), "When the head is enlightened, the limbs are good"; what the Biographical Accounts of Filial Piety (Shishi) call "the moral sense conferred by Heaven and the constant norm held within" is the meaning of the Book of Documents, "adapting to their constant nature"; when the Hidden Rewards for Doing Good (Yinzhi) speaks of doing good and receiving recompense, this is what the Book of Documents says: "Following the right way brings good fortune; following the perverse brings misfortune"; and when the Book of the Five Relationships (Wulun) speaks of governing through the cardinal bonds and constant virtues, this too is what the Book of Documents says: "The invariable human relationships are thus set in order." That they tally with the ancients and follow the same tracks lies precisely in this; fitting indeed is it that they should be transmitted together for ten thousand generations without end! As for their grand outline and overarching purport—such as creating blessings for the people, exhorting people to practice filial piety, encouraging people to do good, and instructing them in human relationships—their essentials do not lie outside of these. Yet filial piety is the crown of the hundred conducts and the root of the myriad good deeds. Although filial piety is spoken of as a single matter, there is no principle of the five relationships that it does not pervade; who could say that filial piety stops at being merely one matter and no more? The Commentary (Zhuan) says: "Because one serves one's parents with filial piety, loyalty can be transferred to the ruler." These words I humbly offer at the conclusion of this essay—I know not whether it may be acceptable?

Question Two
Chen Jiayou 陳嘉猷
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Shao comments: What is answered is detailed, clear, and decisive; reading it fills one with respectful awe. Commendable.

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
考試官修撰林批以古人之知人薦舉為要有學
有識之士也
考試官學士江批策問條答明切是亦忠直敢
言之士也
蓋聞致治之道莫先於薦舉之公尤莫要於知
人之明蓋知人不明則無以察賢否嚴進退薦
舉不公則何以抑奔競杜僥倖而得真才以致
治哉請因明問而條陳之知人之道自古為難
唐堯虞舜皆大聖人也其欲用人必內咨群臣
===
與夫四岳驩兜之舉共工堯知其靜言庸違棄
而不用及其治水之責乃復用鯀者蓋懷山襄
陵之患已迫堯思有以紓一時之急而四岳有
試可乃已之言不得不用之耳禹皐陶猶以知
人為言蓋以誠心愛君恐其或怠於此耳不然
以堯舜之為君豈真難於知人也哉迨及漢唐
之世上焉而為君不可儗於堯舜下焉而為臣
不可儗於禹皐其知人乃若有可取者若相如
之文藻而漢武愛之然不過使之從獵而已李

Examiner Senior Compiler Lin comments: Taking the ancients' discernment of men and recommendation for office as the essential points—this is a scholar of both learning and insight.

Examiner Academician Jiang comments: His item-by-item responses to the policy question are clear and incisive; he too is a loyal, forthright scholar who dares to speak out.

I have heard that in the way of bringing about good governance, nothing comes before impartiality in recommending men for office, and nothing is more crucial than perspicacity in knowing men. For if one is not perspicacious in knowing men, there is no way to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy or to strictly regulate advancement and dismissal; if recommendations are not impartial, how can one curb opportunistic place-seeking, block undeserved advancement, and obtain true talent so as to achieve good governance? Allow me to set this forth item by item in response to your perceptive question.

The way of knowing men has been difficult since antiquity. Yao of Tang and Shun of Yu were both great sages. When they wished to employ men, within the court they invariably consulted all the ministers as well as the Four Peaks. When Huandou recommended Gonggong, Yao knew that he spoke smoothly when quiet but acted perversely when employed, and so cast him aside and did not use him. Yet when it came to the responsibility of controlling the floods, Yao nonetheless employed Gun because the disaster of waters enveloping the mountains and overtopping the hills was already pressing; Yao sought some means to relieve the urgency of the moment, and since the Four Peaks had said, "Try him, and if he succeeds, then stop looking," he had no choice but to employ him. That Yu and Gaoyao still spoke of the difficulty of knowing men was simply out of their sincere love for their sovereign, fearing lest he grow negligent in this regard. Otherwise, with rulers such as Yao and Shun, could it truly have been difficult for them to know men?

When it came down to the ages of Han and Tang, those above who served as rulers could not be compared to Yao and Shun, and those below who served as ministers could not be compared to Yu and Gaoyao. Yet in their knowing of men, there seemed to be aspects worthy of note: for instance, Emperor Wu of Han loved the literary brilliance of Sima Xiangru, yet he did no more than have him attend the imperial hunts; Li…

text:
白之英邁明皇重之然不過任之待詔而已孔
明知魏延之怯不可以為軍師房喬知李緯之
器不足以為尚書然皆天下之常才當時在
位者不過慮一事之不立而不用耳是四人者
豈能有補於天下之治亂也哉有宋盛時公道
大明伊川一布衣耳申國呂公薦為侍講以其
窮神知化有得於聖賢之學也蘇洵一布衣耳歐
陽文忠薦為主簿以其應變成務見於權衡之
書也大臣之薦舉士之受薦若此其可矣恭惟我
===
朝
皇上嗣承
列聖撫御萬邦求賢知人之鑒誠所謂軼唐虞而陋
漢唐矣嘗下
明詔責廷臣各舉所知以資任用然尤未臻治效
者蓋薦舉之法要秉夫至公至明之心內不避
親若謝安之薦謝玄曹彬之薦曹瑋外不避故
若文靖之薦孝肅呂公之薦元城是已奈何奔
競成風士習僥倖司薦舉者或不能如古人知

punctuated: 白之英邁，明皇重之，然不過任之待詔而已；孔明知魏延之怯，不可以為軍師；房喬知李緯之器，不足以為尚書。然皆天下之常才，當時在位者不過慮一事之不立而不用耳。是四人者，豈能有補於天下之治亂也哉？有宋盛時，公道大明：伊川一布衣耳，申國呂公薦為侍講，以其窮神知化，有得於聖賢之學也；蘇洵一布衣耳，歐陽文忠薦為主簿，以其應變成務，見於《權衡》之書也。大臣之薦舉、士之受薦，若此其可矣。恭惟我朝皇上嗣承列聖，撫御萬邦，求賢知人之鑒，誠所謂軼唐、虞而陋漢、唐矣。嘗下明詔，責廷臣各舉所知，以資任用。然尤未臻治效者，蓋薦舉之法，要秉夫至公至明之心：內不避親，若謝安之薦謝玄、曹彬之薦曹瑋；外不避故，若文靖之薦孝肅、呂公之薦元城是已。奈何奔競成風，士習僥倖，司薦舉者或不能如古人知
translation_en:
… Bai ʼs heroic brilliance was valued by Emperor Minghuang (Xuanzong of Tang), yet he merely appointed him as an Expectant Official (daizhao). Kongming (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) knew of Wei Yan 魏延ʼs timidity [?] and that he could not be made an Army Advisor (junshi); Fang Qiao 房喬 (Fang Xuanling 房玄齡) knew that Li Wei 李緯ʼs capacity was insufficient for him to serve as a Minister (shangshu). Yet these were all ordinary talents of the realm, and those in office at the time merely worried that a single matter might fail to be accomplished and so did not employ them. How could these four men have been of any help to the order or disorder of the realm? During the flourishing era of the Song dynasty, the way of impartiality was brilliantly manifest. Yichuan 伊川 (Cheng Yi 程頤) was merely a commoner, yet the Duke of Shen, Lü Gong 呂公 (Lü Gongzhu 呂公著), recommended him as a Lecturer-in-Waiting (shijiang), because he fathomed the spirit and understood transformation, having attained the learning of the sages and worthies. Su Xun 蘇洵 was merely a commoner, yet Ouyang Wenzhong 歐陽文忠 (Ouyang Xiu 歐陽修) recommended him as a Recorder (zhubu), because his ability to respond to changes and accomplish affairs was evident in his book Quanheng (The Balance). When grand ministers recommend and scholars receive recommendations in such a manner, it is truly fitting.

Reverently I reflect that His Majesty of our dynasty has succeeded the line of Imperial Sages and pacifies and governs the myriad states. His discernment in seeking worthies and knowing men truly surpasses that of Tang and Yu and makes Han and Tang look base. He once issued a luminous edict holding the court officials responsible for each recommending those whom they know, so as to provide for appointment and employment. Yet the reason this has still not achieved the full efficacy of good governance is that the method of recommendation requires holding fast to a mind of the utmost impartiality and utmost clarity: internally not avoiding relatives, as when Xie An 謝安 recommended Xie Xuan 謝玄 and Cao Bin 曹彬 recommended Cao Wei 曹瑋; and externally not avoiding old acquaintances, as when Wenzhing 文靖 (Lü Yijian 呂夷簡) recommended Xiaosu 孝肅 (Bao Zheng 包拯) and Lü Gong 呂公 (Lü Gongzhu) recommended Yuancheng 元城 (Liu Anshi 劉安世). How regrettable it is that scrambling for advancement has become the custom, scholars are habituated to seeking undeserved fortune, and those in charge of recommendations are perhaps unable to match the ancients' discernment in knowing…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
人之明靜言庸違者得以倖進廉退方正者無
自登庸甚至援引親故竊位苟祿宜有以發執
事之歎也使今之居廟堂者皆能慎禹皐之知
人如宋諸臣之薦舉闢公道而進恬退勵廉耻
而尚節義則布於有位者莫非正人君子庶可
以資夫唐虞之治以副
皇上宵旰之求致雍熈泰和之治也不難矣愚生不
足以知此執事其進而教之
第三問
===
吳匯
同考試官參政羅 批此策頭緒頗多却能逐一分
辨終則以治人本於修身而修身本於敬必熟
於本領者也
考試官修撰林 批所答詳明且知其要必熟於四書者

人之明靜言庸違者得以倖進廉退方正者無
自登庸甚至援引親故竊位苟祿宜有以發執
事之歎也使今之居廟堂者皆能慎禹皐之知
人如宋諸臣之薦舉闢公道而進恬退勵廉恥
而尚節義則布於有位者莫非正人君子庶可
以資夫唐虞之治以副
皇上宵旰之求致雍熈泰和之治也不難矣愚生不
足以知此執事其進而教之

punctuated:
人之明，靜言庸違者得以倖進，廉退方正者無自登庸；甚至援引親故，竊位苟祿，宜有以發執事之歎也。使今之居廟堂者，皆能慎禹、皐之知人，如宋諸臣之薦舉，闢公道而進恬退，勵廉耻而尚節義，則布於有位者莫非正人君子，庶可以資夫唐、虞之治，以副皇上宵旰之求，致雍熈泰和之治也不難矣。愚生不足以知此，執事其進而教之。

吳匯
同考試官參政羅批：此策頭緒頗多，却能逐一分辨，終則以治人本於修身，而修身本於敬，必熟於本領者也。
考試官修撰林批：所答詳明，且知其要，必熟於《四書》者。
考試官學士江批：羣疑能剖析，舉要以對，足見學識之優。

對：聖賢之立言雖不同，而莫不有其要；學者之為學雖有序，而惟在知其要。盖知要則足以盡
translation_en:
… discernment in knowing men, so that those who speak smoothly when quiet but act perversely when employed are able to advance by luck, while the incorrupt, retiring, upright, and square have no way to ascend to office; it even goes so far as pulling in relatives and old friends, stealing positions and carelessly drawing salaries—no wonder this has prompted Your Excellency's sigh! If those who occupy the court today could all be as careful in knowing men as Yu 禹 and Gao Yao 皐陶 were, and make recommendations like those ministers of the Song dynasty—opening up the way of impartiality and advancing the calm and retiring, encouraging a sense of honor and shame and esteeming integrity and righteousness—then those arrayed in office would all be upright men and gentlemen. Thus they might contribute to a governance like that of Tang 唐 [Yao 堯] and Yu 虞 [Shun 舜], fulfill the Emperor's tireless quest from dawn to dusk, and bring about an era of harmonious and supreme peace without difficulty. This foolish student is inadequate to know such matters; may Your Excellency bring me forward and instruct me.

Wu Hui 吳匯
Comment by Associate Examiner and Administration Vice Commissioner Luo 羅: This policy essay has quite a few threads, yet it manages to distinguish each one in turn, concluding that governing others is rooted in self-cultivation, and self-cultivation is rooted in reverence; he must be one who is well-versed in fundamental principles.
Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Lin 林: The response is detailed and clear, and moreover grasps the essentials; he must be one who is well-versed in the Four Books.

Response: Although the words established by the sages and worthies differ, none lack their essential point; although there is a sequence to how scholars pursue learning, it lies solely in knowing the essential point. For if one knows the essential point, one is able to exhaust…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
博能博而求夫不一之言約而歸於至一之理
則聖賢之道可得矣執事先生發策以四書為
問誠以四書者孔曾思孟相傳之心法正學者
之所當講也愚不敏敢不悉心以對嘗觀大學
一書其言雖博而其始終不出乎敬如格致誠
正之属莫不以敬為主敬非大學之要乎中庸
一書其言雖多而其樞紐不出乎誠如達道達
德九經之属莫不以誠為本誠非中庸之要乎
論語之學在於操存涵養則曾子之三省顏子
===
===
之克復與夫終食不違舞雩詠歸者是已孟子
之學在於體驗充廣則先義後利為善為利之
別與夫充惻隱羞惡之心而仁義不可勝用者
是已曰操存涵養曰體驗充廣又非論語孟子
之要乎然四書之旨固各有要而所以為要者
不外乎修己而已修己之道在論語孔子答子
路問君子則曰修己以敬中庸孔子答哀公問
政則曰修身以道而大學論明德之事則又曰
心正而后身修其言之不同者蓋因其所寓之

論語之學在於操存涵養則曾子之三省顏子
===
之克復與夫終食不違舞雩詠歸者是已孟子
之學在於體驗充廣則先義後利為善為利之
別與夫充惻隱羞惡之心而仁義不可勝用者
是已曰操存涵養曰體驗充廣又非論語孟子
之要乎然四書之旨固各有要而所以為要者
不外乎修已而已修已之道在論語孔子答子
路問君子則曰修已以敬中庸孔子答哀公問
政則曰修身以道而大學論明德之事則又曰
心正而后身修其言之不同者蓋因其所寓之
punctuated:
博。能博而求夫不一之言，約而歸於至一之理，則聖賢之道可得矣。執事先生發策，以《四書》為問，誠以《四書》者，孔、曾、思、孟相傳之心法，正學者之所當講也。愚不敏，敢不悉心以對？
嘗觀《大學》一書，其言雖博，而其始終不出乎敬。如格、致、誠、正之属，莫不以敬為主。敬非《大學》之要乎？《中庸》一書，其言雖多，而其樞紐不出乎誠。如達道、達德、九經之属，莫不以誠為本。誠非《中庸》之要乎？《論語》之學在於操存涵養，則曾子之三省、顏子之克復，與夫終食不違、舞雩詠歸者是已。《孟子》之學在於體驗充廣，則先義後利、為善為利之別，與夫充惻隱、羞惡之心而仁義不可勝用者是已。曰操存涵養，曰體驗充廣，又非《論語》、《孟子》之要乎？
然《四書》之旨，固各有要，而所以為要者，不外乎修己而已。修己之道，在《論語》孔子答子路問君子，則曰「修己以敬」；《中庸》孔子答哀公問政，則曰「修身以道」；而《大學》論明德之事，則又曰「心正而后身修」。其言之不同者，蓋因其所寓之
translation_en:
… breadth. When one is able to be broad in inquiry, seeking out the diverse sayings, and then condense and reduce them to the supremely unified principle, the Way of the sages and worthies can be attained. You, sir, in setting forth this policy question, have asked about the Four Books, truly because the Four Books contain the method of the mind-and-heart transmitted successively by Confucius (Kongzi 孔子), Zengzi 曾子, Zisi 子思, and Mencius (Mengzi 孟子), which is precisely what scholars ought to investigate and discuss. Though I am dull-witted, how dare I not devote my whole mind to replying?

I have observed that in the Great Learning (Daxue 大學), although its words are broad, from beginning to end it does not go beyond reverence (jing 敬). Matters such as investigating things, extending knowledge, making the intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind all take reverence as their master. Is reverence not the essential point of the Great Learning? In the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong 中庸), although its words are many, its pivot does not go beyond sincerity (cheng 誠). Matters such as the universal ways, the universal virtues, and the nine standard rules all take sincerity as their foundation. Is sincerity not the essential point of the Doctrine of the Mean? The learning of the Analects (Lunyu 論語) lies in grasping, preserving, and nurturing one's mind; such are Zengzi's daily examination on three points, Yanzi's 顏子 overcoming the self and returning to propriety, as well as not acting contrary to benevolence even for the space of a single meal, and singing on the way home from the rain dance altars. The learning of the Mencius (Mengzi 孟子) lies in personal verification and extension; such are putting righteousness first and profit last, the distinction between doing good and seeking profit, as well as extending the mind of compassion and of shame and dislike until benevolence and righteousness are more than can be used. What are called "grasping, preserving, and nurturing" and "personal verification and extension"—are these not in turn the essential points of the Analects and the Mencius?

Yet while the purport of each of the Four Books indeed has its own essential point, that by which it serves as the essential point is nothing other than cultivating the self. As for the way of cultivating the self: in the Analects, when Confucius answered Zilu's 子路 question about the noble man, he said, "He cultivates himself with reverence"; in the Doctrine of the Mean, when Confucius answered Duke Ai's (Ai Gong 哀公) question about governance, he said, "One cultivates the person by means of the Way"; and when the Great Learning discusses the matter of illustrating illustrious virtue, it further says, "When the mind is rectified, the person is cultivated." That their words differ is simply because the contexts in which they are lodged…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
不同耳然要其歸言之則道原於心而心之也
敬欲盡修身之道者莫先於敬能以敬為以人
以心為體道之原以道為修身之本所謂正心
修身者可以因其一以該其餘矣修身而後治
人治人之道在論語孔子答子路之問則曰修
已以安百姓大學論新民之事則曰國治而后
天下平子思論中庸之極功則曰君子篤恭而
天下平至孟子論為治本於孝弟則又曰人人
親其親長其長而天下平其言之不同者亦因
===
其所指之不同耳然要其歸而論之則天下之
本在國國之本在家家之本在身欲盡治人之
效者莫先於修身能修其身則家無不齊國無
不治而天下無不平亦可以篤近而舉遠矣論
至於是則知治人必本於修身而修身必本於
敬學者誠能從事於論語操存涵養之功孟子
體驗充廣之事以求至於中庸之誠大學之敬
則此所謂修已以敬極而至於篤恭而天下平
不外是矣愚也窮經而不能知其要問學而不

不同耳然要其歸言之則道原於心而心之也
敬欲盡修身之道者莫先於敬能以敬爲以人
以心爲體道之原以道爲修身之本所謂正心
修身者可以因其一以該其餘矣修身而後治

天下平子思論中庸之極功則曰君子篤恭而
天下平至孟子論爲治本於孝弟則又曰人人
親其親長其長而天下平其言之不同者亦因
===
其所指之不同耳然要其歸而論之則天下之
本在國國之本在家家之本在身欲盡治人之
效者莫先於修身能修其身則家無不齊國無
不治而天下無不平亦可以篤近而舉遠矣論
至於是則知治人必本於修身而修身必本於
敬學者誠能從事於論語操存涵養之功孟子
體驗充廣之事以求至於中庸之誠大學之敬
則此所謂修已以敬極而至於篤恭而天下平
不外是矣愚也竊經而不能知其要問學而不
punctuated: 不同耳。然要其歸言之，則道原於心，而心之也敬，欲盡修身之道者，莫先於敬。能以敬為以人，以心為體道之原，以道為修身之本，所謂「正心、修身」者，可以因其一以該其餘矣。修身而後治人，治人之道，在《論語》孔子答子路之問，則曰：「修已以安百姓。」《大學》論新民之事，則曰：「國治而后天下平。」子思論中庸之極功，則曰：「君子篤恭而天下平。」至《孟子》論為治本於孝弟，則又曰：「人人親其親，長其長，而天下平。」其言之不同者，亦因其所指之不同耳。然要其歸而論之，則天下之本在國，國之本在家，家之本在身，欲盡治人之效者，莫先於修身。能修其身，則家無不齊，國無不治，而天下無不平，亦可以篤近而舉遠矣。論至於是，則知治人必本於修身，而修身必本於敬。學者誠能從事於《論語》操存涵養之功、《孟子》體驗充廣之事，以求至於《中庸》之誠、《大學》之敬，則此所謂「修已以敬」，極而至於「篤恭而天下平」，不外是矣。愚也窮經而不能知其要，問學而不
translation_en:
…differences in what they are lodged in. Yet if we sum up their ultimate conclusion, the Way originates in the mind, and [what governs?] the mind is reverence [?]. For one who wishes to fulfill the Way of cultivating the person, nothing takes precedence over reverence. If one is able to take reverence as [the master of the mind?], take the mind as the source for embodying the Way, and take the Way as the foundation for cultivating the person, then what is called "rectifying the mind and cultivating the person" can through this single principle encompass all the rest.

Only after cultivating the person does one govern others. As for the Way of governing others: in the Analects (Lunyu), when Confucius answered Zilu's question, he said, "Cultivate oneself to bring peace to the common people." When the Great Learning (Daxue) discusses the matter of renewing the people, it says, "When the state is rightly governed, thereafter the world is at peace." When Zisi discusses the ultimate achievement of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong), he says, "The superior man is篤恭 (earnestly reverent) and the world is at peace." And when the Mencius (Mengzi) discusses how governance is rooted in filial piety and fraternal respect, it says, "If everyone loves their parents and respects their elders, then the world will be at peace." That their words differ is likewise simply due to the differences in what they point toward. Yet if we sum up their ultimate conclusion and discuss it, the root of the world lies in the state, the root of the state lies in the family, and the root of the family lies in the person; for one who wishes to fulfill the efficacy of governing others, nothing takes precedence over cultivating the person. If one is able to cultivate one's person, then no family will fail to be regulated, no state will fail to be rightly governed, and the world will never fail to be at peace; thus one can be earnest in what is near and thereby uplift what is far.

When our discussion reaches this point, we know that governing others must be rooted in cultivating the person, and cultivating the person must be rooted in reverence. If the scholar is truly able to engage in the work of preserving and nurturing the mind taught in the Analects and the task of personal realization and extension taught in the Mencius, seeking thereby to attain the sincerity of the Doctrine of the Mean and the reverence of the Great Learning, then what is here called "cultivating oneself with reverence," reaching its utmost in "being earnestly reverent and the world being at peace," is nothing other than this. Ignorant as I am, I have studied the Classics exhaustively yet cannot grasp their essentials, and have inquired into learning yet cannot…

能究其歸管見如斯惟進教之幸甚
第四問
許倫
同考試官教授謝批策本覌人博學識見對

能究其歸，管見如斯，惟進教之，幸甚。

第四問

許倫

同考試官教授謝批：策本覌人博學識見，對者寥寥，惟此作援引考據，節節詳明，必老於學者也。

同考試官侍講劉批：策問政欲觀士子有用之學，此答前敘科目得人，古今無間，已見斟酌；後復引古名賢事，望大臣為之倡以救時弊，尤見學識。

考試官修撰林批：科目之得人也尚矣，龜山必有為而言也。觀此策終篇所答，必能法古人以為科目重者歟！可羨，可羨。

考試官學士江批：策問歷舉古今之科目得人與否，敷答詳明，議論正大，有學有識之士也。

論科目之得人，無間於古今；論人材之賢否，亦無間於古今。盖科目，人材之所由進，而其人之有賢否者，習之相遠，古今皆然也，夫豈繫於科
translation_en:
… unable to fathom its ultimate conclusion. Such is my humble view; I would count it the greatest fortune if I might be brought forward for instruction.

Fourth Policy Question

Xu Lun 許倫

Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Xie 謝: Policy questions are fundamentally intended to observe a person's breadth of learning and insight, yet few respondents do them justice. Only this essay cites and verifies sources with clear detail in every section; its author must be a seasoned scholar.

Comment by Associate Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting Liu 劉: The policy question was precisely intended to observe the practical learning of the candidates. In the first part, this answer recounts how the recruitment of talent through the examination categories shows no gap between antiquity and the present, already demonstrating balanced judgment; later, it again cites the deeds of famous worthies of antiquity, hoping that great ministers will take the lead in remedying current abuses, which even more clearly displays learning and insight.

Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Lin 林: Recruitment of talent through the examination categories has a long history; Guishan 龜山 [Yang Shi 楊時] must have had a specific reason for speaking as he did. Judging from what this policy essay answers through to the end, its author will surely be able to emulate the ancients and thereby bring weight to the examination system! Admirable, truly admirable.

Comment by Examiner and Academician Jiang 江: The policy question successively raised the issue of whether the examination categories of antiquity and the present succeeded in obtaining talent. This candidate sets forth his reply in clear detail and his arguments are upright and grand—a scholar possessing both learning and insight.

If we discuss the recruitment of talent through the examination categories, there is no difference between antiquity and the present; if we discuss the worthiness or unworthiness of human talent, there is likewise no difference between antiquity and the present. For the examination categories are the means by which men of talent advance, whereas the fact that among these men some are worthy and some unworthy comes from how far apart their habits and practices grow—this has been true in both antiquity and the present. How could it be tied to the examination…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
目哉粤自鄉舉里選之法廢而明經進士之科
起士之抱寸長挾一藝不得以自效者皆於是而
售焉然其得人之盛莫過於唐宋而尤莫過於
國朝也姑以唐宋得人論之如裴度之出將入相

punctuated: 目哉？粤自鄉舉里選之法廢，而明經、進士之科起，士之抱寸長、挾一藝、不得以自效者，皆於是而售焉。然其得人之盛，莫過於唐、宋，而尤莫過於國朝也。姑以唐、宋得人論之：如裴度之出將入相，收功淮、蔡，而四夷仰其名；李絳之捜次成敗，其種五十，而朝廷信其言；餉錢百萬，拒而不納，陸贄之廉介可尚也；父任執政，不就廷試，韓維之恬退可嘉也；出刺潮州，鱷魚南徙，韓愈之除民害，又何其不可及也！得人如斯，誠足為科目重矣。求之於今，内列侍從之任，外受方岳之寄，與凡有位于列者，如裴、如李、如陸、如韓，其人不少。彼其忠義足以匡時，風節足以勵俗，利澤施於人，名聲昭于時，推而較之，何下彼哉？其間有遇事退縮，而致身之義有乖；阿諛取容，而忠讜之論鮮聞；務貪求奔競，而莫之愧；視民隱物怪，而莫之恤者，誠由太平日久，士習奢縱，知富貴而不知功名，急小利而忘大義故耳。然豈獨今之時為然？向之楊嗣復、楊虞卿之徒，劉禹錫、王涯…
translation_en: …the examination categories? Ever since the system of local recommendation and village selection was abolished and the examination categories of Classicist (mingjing) and Metropolitan Graduate (jinshi) arose, scholars who possessed even a modest talent or mastered a single art, yet previously had no means to prove themselves, have all found recognition through this path. Yet the flourishing of talent thus recruited was never greater than in the Tang and Song dynasties, and above all, never greater than in our own dynasty. Let us first discuss the recruitment of talent in the Tang and Song: for instance, Pei Du 裴度 went forth as a general and returned as a Grand Councilor, achieving victory in Huai 淮 and Cai 蔡 while the four barbarian peoples looked up to his name; Li Jiang 李絳 compiled historical successes and failures under fifty categories, and the court trusted his words; when presented with a million cash in provisions, Lu Zhi 陸贄 refused to accept it—how admirable was his incorruptible integrity! Because his father held the post of Grand Councilor, Han Wei 韓維 declined to sit for the Palace Examination—how praiseworthy was his unassuming modesty! Sent out as Prefect of Chaozhou 潮州, Han Yu 韓愈 caused the crocodiles to migrate south—how unmatchable was his elimination of harm for the people! Recruiting men such as these was truly enough to bring honor to the examination categories. Seeking their likes today—among those ranked within the court in attendant posts, those entrusted abroad with provincial administration, and all who hold office in the official ranks—there are not a few who are like Pei, Li, Lu, and Han. Their loyalty and righteousness suffice to rectify the age, their moral integrity suffices to inspire custom, their beneficence is bestowed upon the people, and their renown shines forth in their time; if we examine and compare them, how are they inferior to those predecessors? Yet among them there are some who shrink back when confronted with difficulties, violating the duty of devoting one's life to the sovereign; who flatter to curry favor, so that loyal and forthright counsel is rarely heard; who busy themselves with greedy pursuit and self-seeking competition without a sense of shame; and who look upon the sufferings of the people and portents in nature without compassion. This is truly because peace has endured for so long that scholars have grown accustomed to luxury and indulgence, knowing only wealth and rank while ignoring meritorious achievement and reputation, rushing after petty gain while forgetting great moral duty. Yet how could this be true only of the present day? In times past, men of the ilk of Yang Sifu 楊嗣復 and Yang Yuqing 楊虞卿, and the sort of Liu Yuxi 劉禹錫 and Wang Ya 王涯…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
之輩亦由是出則人材之有賢否從古然也尚
何古今人不相及與所以求之者未精哉今欲
革其故使得人皆如前之諸公莫先於敦士風
以勵其廉耻之操重名節以作其忠義之氣而
尤在大臣有以倡之也誠使倡之者有如富弼
遇契丹之警即慷慨請行則人皆有所奮發亦
何有於遇事退縮乎有如蘇洵父子之不避權
貴極詆新法則人皆有所感激亦何有於懷詐
為佞乎有如李沆之所居陋巷廳事前僅容旋
馬則人皆以儉德相尚而貪自無矣有如司馬
公重劉器之不通書問特薦進之則人知恬退
為高而請託自息矣有如曾公亮之急於去民
所疾苦則人有所視效而民患自無不除矣誠
如是則不惟見科目之得人抑亦見人材之有
用而龜山楊氏之說有不驗矣愚也蒙
朝廷作養之恩荷執事策之之意前所論為科目
玷者固非所志矣為科目重者非曰能之願學
焉進教之幸甚

punctuated: 之輩，亦由是出。則人材之有賢否，從古然也。尚何古今人不相及，與所以求之者未精哉？今欲革其故，使得人皆如前之諸公，莫先於敦士風以勵其廉耻之操，重名節以作其忠義之氣，而尤在大臣有以倡之也。誠使倡之者，有如富弼遇契丹之警，即慷慨請行，則人皆有所奮發，亦何有於遇事退縮乎？有如蘇洵父子之不避權貴，極詆新法，則人皆有所感激，亦何有於懷詐為佞乎？有如李沆之所居陋巷，廳事前僅容旋馬，則人皆以儉德相尚，而貪自無矣。有如司馬公重劉器之不通書問，特薦進之，則人知恬退為高，而請託自息矣。有如曾公亮之急於去民所疾苦，則人有所視效，而民患自無不除矣。誠如是，則不惟見科目之得人，抑亦見人材之有用，而龜山楊氏之說有不驗矣。愚也蒙朝廷作養之恩，荷執事策之之意，前所論為科目玷者，固非所志矣；為科目重者，非曰能之，願學焉。進教之，幸甚。
translation_en: … and their ilk also emerged through these same examinations. That men of talent include both the worthy and the unworthy has been so since antiquity. How then can it be that men of the present do not measure up to those of the past, or that the means of seeking them are not sufficiently refined? If today we wish to reform old habits so that all the men we obtain are like the worthies mentioned previously, nothing is more urgent than cultivating the ethos of the literati to encourage their sense of integrity and shame, and prizing reputation and moral fortitude to rouse their spirit of loyalty and righteousness; and above all, this depends on the great ministers taking the lead. Truly, if among those who lead there are men like Fu Bi 富弼, who upon encountering the Qidan alarm generously requested to go on the mission himself, then everyone would be inspired to exert themselves—how could there be any shrinking back when confronted with difficulties? If there are men like Su Xun 蘇洵 and his sons, who did not shy away from the powerful and noble in utterly denouncing the New Policies, then everyone would be moved and stirred—how could there be any harboring of deceit to practice flattery? If there are men like Li Hang 李沆, who lived in a humble lane with a hall front barely wide enough for a horse to turn around, then everyone would esteem the virtue of frugality, and greed would naturally vanish. If there are men like Lord Sima [Sima Guang 司馬光], who valued Liu Qizhi 劉器之 [Liu Anshi 劉安世] for not sending letters of greeting and specially recommended him for promotion, then people would recognize that quiet modesty is lofty, and private solicitation for favors would naturally cease. If there are men like Zeng Gongliang 曾公亮, who was urgent in removing the sufferings of the people, then others would have a model to emulate, and the afflictions of the people would naturally all be eliminated. If it is truly like this, then not only will we see the examination categories obtaining the right men, we will also see that men of talent are put to practical use, and the assertion of Master Yang of Guishan [Yang Shi 楊時] will prove unfounded. Ignorant as I am, having received the grace of the court's nurturing and training and been favored with Your Excellencies' intent in posing this policy question, to be among those discussed earlier who bring blemish to the examination categories is certainly not my aspiration; as for being among those who bring honor to the examination categories, I do not say that I am capable of it, but I wish to learn how. I would be most fortunate if you would advance and instruct me.

嘗謂用兵之道莫先於選將而選將之要惟在
===
於得人古云有必勝之將無必勝之民又云君
不擇將以其國與敵也由是而言可不謹諸古
者國家雖安必常選將然得兵十萬不如一將
是知將不可不選也選將之道惟審其才之可
用不以賤而疎不以罪而棄若管仲舉於射鉤

累李勣收於降附是數人者皆卒能建立大勳

嘗謂用兵之道，莫先於選將，而選將之要，惟在於得人。古云：「有必勝之將，無必勝之民。」又云：「君不擇將，以其國與敵也。」由是而言，可不謹諸？古者國家雖安，必常選將，然得兵十萬，不如一將，是知將不可不選也。選將之道，惟審其才之可用，不以賤而疎，不以罪而棄。若管仲舉於射鉤，穰苴拔於寒微，韓信之怯懦，衛青之人奴，諸葛亮之不親戎服，杜預之不便鞍馬，李靖收於罪累，李勣收於降附。是數人者，皆卒能建立大勳，助成王伯之業，初豈以其形貌閥閲計其間哉？
translation_en:
Fifth Question
Xiang Jie 相傑
Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary Qian: On the topic of selecting generals, most writers were constrained by the historical facts; only this paper answered point by point without omission, amply demonstrating scholarship and insight.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Senior Compiler Li: The narration of historical events is detailed and clear, and the wording is concise and to the point. Acceptable.
Comment by Examiner and Senior Compiler Lin: The point-by-point answers are precise and clear, and furthermore grasp the essentials of selecting generals. Most commendable, most commendable!
Comment by Examiner and Academician Jiang: The policy essay is able to answer what was asked. Acceptable.

I have heard it said that in the way of employing troops, nothing takes precedence over selecting generals, and the essence of selecting generals lies solely in obtaining the right men. An ancient saying goes: "There are generals who are certain to win, but there are no common people who are certain to win." Another saying goes: "A ruler who fails to choose his generals properly hands his state over to the enemy." Viewed in this light, how can one not be cautious about it? In antiquity, even when the state was at peace, generals were always selected; indeed, acquiring a hundred thousand soldiers is not as good as acquiring a single general. From this we know that generals must be carefully selected. The way of selecting generals lies solely in examining whether their talents are usable—not alienating them because of humble status, nor discarding them because of past offenses. For instance, Guan Zhong 管仲 was promoted after shooting the ruler's belt buckle; Rangju 穰苴 was elevated from humble obscurity; Han Xin 韓信 was once considered timid and cowardly; Wei Qing 衛青 was another man's bondservant; Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮 did not personally wear military attire; Du Yu 杜預 was not skilled in saddle and horse; Li Jing 李靖 was taken in despite being implicated in offenses; and Li Ji 李勣 was accepted from among those who surrendered. All of these several men were ultimately able to establish great merit and assist in accomplishing the enterprises of true kings and hegemons. In the beginning, how could anyone have calculated among them on the basis of their physical appearance or family pedigree?

text:
至若選将以五才為體五謹為用所謂五才曰
知曰信曰仁曰勇曰嚴非知無以料敵應機非
信無以訓人率下非仁無以附衆撫士非勇無
以决謀合戰非嚴無以服彊齊衆五謹者曰理
曰備曰果曰誡曰約理者理衆如理寡備者出
門如見敵果者見敵不懷生誡者雖克如始戰
約者法令省而不煩人君知此十者而猶慮取
人之難又設九驗之言詞以考之九術之法例
以復之所謂九驗者遠使之以觀其忠近使之
===
以觀其恭繁使之以觀其能卒然問之以觀其
智急與之期以觀其信與之貨財以觀其仁告
之以危以觀其節醉之以酒以觀其態雜之以
處以觀其色所謂九術者知其飢寒見其勞苦
之謂仁将有死而榮無生而辱之謂義将貴而
不驕勝而不逸非禮将乎轉禍為福因危立勝
非智将乎賞不踰時刑不擇貴信将也足輕戎
馬力踰千夫步将也臨高立險馳射若飛騎将
也氣凌三軍志輕彊虜非猛将而何見賢

punctuated: 至若選将，以五才為體，五謹為用。所謂五才：曰知，曰信，曰仁，曰勇，曰嚴。非知無以料敵應機，非信無以訓人率下，非仁無以附衆撫士，非勇無以决謀合戰，非嚴無以服彊齊衆。五謹者：曰理，曰備，曰果，曰誡，曰約。理者，理衆如理寡；備者，出門如見敵；果者，見敵不懷生；誡者，雖克如始戰；約者，法令省而不煩。人君知此十者，而猶慮取人之難，又設九驗之言詞以考之，九術之法例以復之。所謂九驗者：遠使之以觀其忠，近使之以觀其恭，繁使之以觀其能，卒然問之以觀其智，急與之期以觀其信，與之貨財以觀其仁，告之以危以觀其節，醉之以酒以觀其態，雜之以處以觀其色。所謂九術者：知其飢寒、見其勞苦之謂仁将，有死而榮、無生而辱之謂義将，貴而不驕、勝而不逸，非禮将乎？轉禍為福、因危立勝，非智将乎？賞不踰時、刑不擇貴，信将也；足輕戎馬、力踰千夫，步将也；臨高立險、馳射若飛，騎将也；氣凌三軍、志輕彊虜，非猛将而何？見賢
translation_en: As for selecting generals, one takes the five talents as the substance and the five cautions as the function. What are called the five talents are: wisdom, trustworthiness, benevolence, courage, and strictness. Without wisdom, there is no way to assess the enemy and respond to opportunities; without trustworthiness, there is no way to instruct people and lead subordinates; without benevolence, there is no way to win the allegiance of the multitude and comfort the soldiers; without courage, there is no way to decide upon plans and join battle; without strictness, there is no way to subdue the strong and bring order to the multitude. The five cautions are: order, preparedness, resoluteness, vigilance, and simplicity. Order means governing the many as one governs the few; preparedness means going out the gate as though facing the enemy; resoluteness means facing the enemy without clinging to life; vigilance means that even after winning a victory, one acts as if just beginning to fight; simplicity means that laws and orders are concise and not burdensome. Even when a ruler knows these ten principles, he still worries about the difficulty of selecting men, and so he further establishes the words of the nine tests to examine them, and the standards of the nine methods to verify them. What are called the nine tests are: sending him on distant missions to observe his loyalty; employing him close at hand to observe his respectfulness; assigning him complex tasks to observe his ability; questioning him suddenly to observe his wisdom; making urgent appointments with him to observe his trustworthiness; entrusting him with goods and wealth to observe his benevolence; informing him of danger to observe his integrity; making him drunk with wine to observe his demeanor; placing him in mixed company to observe his propriety toward women. What are called the nine methods are: knowing the troops' hunger and cold and seeing their toil and hardship is called a benevolent general; accepting death with honor rather than life with disgrace is called a righteous general; being noble without arrogance and victorious without indulgence—is this not a general of propriety? Turning disaster into good fortune and wresting victory from peril—is this not a wise general? Rewarding without delay and punishing without sparing the noble—this is a trustworthy general; being swifter of foot than warhorses and surpassing a thousand men in strength—this is an infantry general; scaling heights and standing on perilous ground, galloping and shooting as if flying—this is a cavalry general; having a spirit that towers over the Three Armies and a will that scorns strong foes—what is this if not a fierce general? Seeing the worthy…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
思齊從諫如流非大將而何然將之伎能不一
局力不齊有𠩄謂十人之將者焉有𠩄謂百人
之將者焉有𠩄謂千人萬人之將者焉又𠩄謂
十萬百萬人之將者焉是皆因其力勝是任而
知其才器之有高下也然知將之為利而不知
將有五危七過之害不可也曰死可殺曰生可
虜曰忿速可侮曰廉潔可辱曰愛民可煩非五
危乎有勇而輕死者可暴有急而心速者可乆
有仁而不忍者可煩有貪而好利者可遺之類
===
非十過乎此又選將者之𠩄當知也今我
國家方注意選將盖有其人矣伊欲其克敵制勝
皆如古之名將迅掃千里以痛快人心莫若澄
其心如水鑑平其誠如權衡則真偽不能逃於
觀察小大不能遺於稱訂尚何不可用之將哉
管子曰王者不能知人害伯也知而不能用害
伯也用而不能任害伯也任而不能信害伯也
既信而使小人參之害伯也然能信在於能任
能任在於能用能用在於能知是則人君選將

能任在於能用能用在於能知是則人君選將
punctuated: 思齊，從諫如流，非大將而何？然將之伎能不一，局力不齊，有𠩄謂十人之將者焉，有𠩄謂百人之將者焉，有𠩄謂千人、萬人之將者焉，又𠩄謂十萬、百萬人之將者焉。是皆因其力勝是任，而知其才器之有高下也。然知將之為利，而不知將有五危、七過之害，不可也。曰死可殺，曰生可虜，曰忿速可侮，曰廉潔可辱，曰愛民可煩，非五危乎？有勇而輕死者可暴，有急而心速者可乆，有仁而不忍者可煩，有貪而好利者可遺之類，非十過乎？此又選將者之𠩄當知也。今我國家方注意選將，盖有其人矣。伊欲其克敵制勝，皆如古之名將，迅掃千里以痛快人心，莫若澄其心如水鑑，平其誠如權衡，則真偽不能逃於觀察，小大不能遺於稱訂，尚何不可用之將哉？《管子》曰：「王者不能知人，害伯也；知而不能用，害伯也；用而不能任，害伯也；任而不能信，害伯也；既信而使小人參之，害伯也。」然能信在於能任，能任在於能用，能用在於能知。是則人君選將…
translation_en:
…[seeing the worthy and] thinking to equal them, and following remonstrance as smoothly as flowing water—what is this if not a grand general? Yet the skills of generals are not uniform, and their capacities and strengths are not equal. There are those called generals of ten men; there are those called generals of a hundred men; there are those called generals of a thousand or ten thousand men; and there are also those called generals of a hundred thousand or a million men. In all these cases, it is by their strength being equal to the responsibility that one knows the higher or lower grades of their talent and capacity. Yet to know the advantages that generals bring, while not knowing the harms of the five fatal flaws and seven failings of generals, is impermissible. If reckless of death, he can be slain; if desperate to live, he can be captured; if quick to anger, he can be provoked by insult; if puritanical regarding his honor, he can be disgraced; if overly fond of the people, he can be worn down with trouble—are these not the five fatal flaws? Those who are brave and take death lightly can be undone by violence; those who are hasty and impatient at heart can be worn down by delay; those who are benevolent and cannot bear to inflict suffering can be harassed; those who are greedy and fond of profit can be bribed—are such things not the ten [sic, seven] failings? This too is what one who selects generals ought to know.

Now our dynasty is currently paying close attention to the selection of generals, and surely such men exist. If we wish them to vanquish the enemy and secure victory, all like the famous generals of antiquity, swiftly sweeping clear a thousand li to the great satisfaction of men's hearts, nothing is better than to clarify one's mind like a water mirror and level one's sincerity like a steelyard and balance. Then the genuine and the false will not be able to escape observation, and the small and the great will not be overlooked in weighing and assessment—what general, then, could not be employed? The Guanzi says: "If a ruler cannot know men, it is harmful to hegemony; to know them and not be able to employ them is harmful to hegemony; to employ them and not be able to entrust them with responsibility is harmful to hegemony; to entrust them with responsibility and not be able to trust them is harmful to hegemony; once trusting them, to allow petty men to interfere with them is harmful to hegemony." Yet being able to trust lies in being able to entrust with responsibility; being able to entrust with responsibility lies in being able to employ; and being able to employ lies in being able to know. Thus, in a ruler's selection of generals…

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

Worthy men of talent are the foundation for bringing about good governance. Since antiquity, when emperors and kings have ruled All under Heaven, the means by which they achieved the flourishing governance of harmonious peace and supreme concord was never other than relying on such men to govern together with them. Now, worthy men of talent exist in every age; yet there must be a proper method for educating them and a proper art for selecting them, and only then can all the genuine talent in the realm be fully obtained and employed. Reflecting deeply upon Our Sacred Dynasty: it examines antiquity in order to govern, venerating Confucians and prizing the Way. In establishing schools to nurture outstanding talents, it instructs them in classical scholarship so as to illuminate the Way, and tests them in literary composition so as to bring forth their inner store of learning. In instituting the examination categories to promote the worthy, it grounds them in the expositions of the Classics in order to seek their substance, and supplements these with discourses and policy questions in order to observe their practical applicability. The means by which they are educated and selected are both comprehensive and refined! Successive Sacred Emperors have carried on the heritage, all following this path. The scholars of the realm,…

translation_en:
…steeped in the long nurturing of sage benevolence, have all attained accomplishment. In flourishing abundance they are arrayed at court and in the provinces; great worthies and noble men who discourse on the Way and broaden transformation, who establish merit and uphold integrity, have all emerged from this. Truly, is this not what Guishan (Yang Shi 楊時) meant when he said that "men of outstanding talent advance through it"?

In the second month of spring in the year following His Majesty's accession and the change of reign era to Jingtai (1451), the year of the triennial examination, the Ministry of Rites, in accordance with established precedent, assembled the tribute scholars (gongshi) of the realm and examined them. His Majesty commanded your servant [Jiang] Yuan 江淵 to preside over the examination, and your servant [Lin] Wen 林文 had the undeserved honor of participating therein. At the time, those who sat for the examination numbered more than two thousand two hundred men; selecting those whose essays conformed to the Classics, we obtained two hundred men—a careful selection indeed. What is recorded in the Classics is the Way of the Sages. When the Classics are illuminated, the Way is illuminated; when the Way is illuminated…

title: 景泰二年會試錄
text:
則發諸文者斯弗畔於道今
觀諸賢士發諸文以應科目
之求者既皆弗畔於道由是
以其道事君則忠以其道治
民則仁以其道建勳立節則
必振耀當時垂聲於後世是
誠不負長育之仁不負科目
===
得實才之用矣苟於所用不
本於所學所行弗踐於所言
以自離於道則今日之所取
者虛文耳貽主司不明之譏
殆難免夫文亦由科目而進
叨祿無補因序于錄後故舉
以為諸賢士勸且以自警云

punctuated: 則發諸文者斯弗畔於道。今觀諸賢士，發諸文以應科目之求者，既皆弗畔於道；由是以其道事君則忠，以其道治民則仁，以其道建勳立節，則必振耀當時，垂聲於後世。是誠不負長育之仁，不負科目得實才之用矣。苟於所用不本於所學，所行弗踐於所言，以自離於道，則今日之所取者虛文耳，貽主司不明之譏，殆難免夫！文亦由科目而進，叨祿無補，因序于錄後，故舉以為諸賢士勸，且以自警云。
translation_en: …then what is expressed in writing will not depart from the Way. Looking now at all you worthy scholars, what you have expressed in your compositions to answer the demands of the examination system does not depart from the Way. If from this point onward you use this Way to serve the ruler, you will be loyal; if you use this Way to govern the people, you will be benevolent; if you use this Way to establish merit and uphold integrity, you will surely shine forth in your own time and leave a reputation for posterity. Truly, this will not betray the court's benevolent nurturing, nor will it betray the examination system's purpose of obtaining genuine talent for practical use. If, however, in how you are employed you do not base yourselves on what you have learned, and in what you do you fail to live up to what you have said, thereby alienating yourselves from the Way, then what has been selected today is nothing more than empty rhetoric, and it will be almost impossible to escape bringing upon the Examiners the ridicule of lacking discernment! I, Lin Wen 林文, also advanced through the examination system, yet I have undeservedly drawn a salary without making any contribution. Therefore, in writing this postface at the end of the record, I raise these points to encourage all you worthy scholars, and also as an admonition to myself.
